news.title: JD Vance 'Wrangling' With the Decision to Run for President After 'Disappointing' Midterm Election, Veep Ally Claims
news.text:
Vice President JD Vance is struggling with whether to run for president in 2028 following Republicans' midterm election losses, with allies telling CNN that he remains undecided, RadarOnline.com can reveal.

CNN White House correspondent Alayna Treene reported Friday, November 12, that conversations with approximately a dozen Vance allies and advisers revealed uncertainty about his presidential ambitions.JD Vance Allies Reveal Uncertainty"They described someone who is really wrangling with this decision over his future political ambitions, the fracturing that we saw of the MAGA coalition," Treene said.

Treene also cited the demands of fatherhood as a consideration for Vance, who welcomed his fourth child with his wife, Usha, in July.

Treene said Vance remains committed to rebuilding the political movement that helped return President Donald Trump to the White House in 2024, although he has not decided whether he wants to lead it.'The Reason We Lost is the War'The ongoing war with Iran has emerged as another factor in Vance's political calculations.

One Vance ally told CNN that the conflict could complicate the presidential ambitions of any Republican, warning that the party must resolve the war before the next election.

The vice president blamed the conflict for the midterm defeats in a lengthy statement on X.

"The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night," Vance wrote. "And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there."Other Republicans Looking to Run for PrezVance's uncertainty comes as several prominent Republicans consider their own presidential ambitions, including Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Texas Sen. Ted Cruz, and Georgia Gov. Brian Kemp.

DeSantis, who unsuccessfully challenged Trump for the 2024 Republican nomination, described the midterm defeats as an "extinction-level event for Republicans."The History of Veeps Running For PresidentOnly four sitting vice presidents have won an election directly to the presidency.

John Adams became the first in 1796, followed by Thomas Jefferson in 1800, Martin Van Buren in 1836, and George H.W. Bush in 1988.

Several other sitting vice presidents were unsuccessful as Richard Nixon lost to John F. Kennedy in 1960, Hubert Humphrey lost to Nixon in 1968, and Al Gore lost to George W. Bush in 2000. Most recently, Vice President Kamala Harris lost the 2024 presidential election to Trump.

Former vice presidents have successfully returned to win the White House, with Nixon winning in 1968, eight years after leaving office, and Joe Biden defeating Trump in 2020, four years after completing his vice presidency under Barack Obama.
news.summary: Vice President JD Vance is struggling with whether to run for president in 2028 following Republicans' 2026 midterm election losses.
news.author: Patrick Previty

news.title: The Politician-to-Podcaster Pipeline Is Getting Crowded
news.text:
Did you catch the latest episode of Inside CentCom? What about This is Gavin Newsom? Did you listen to Hold These Truths with Dan Crenshaw? Well, if you've somehow run out of pod content by politicians, you will soon be able to tune into World War Chi, a podcast by 28-year-old New York City Councilmember Chi Ossé.

Ossé, a member of the Democratic Socialists of America, will be hosting a show for Crooked Media, the media company founded by the Pod Save America hosts, Vulture reported last week. Ossé told Vulture he would squeeze in recording sessions on Saturday or Sunday evenings and that the show will mostly cover cultural topics. Still, there will "be a slow IV drip of socialism throughout each episode," he told Vulture. 

If a "slow IV drip of socialism" is not your speed, you can listen to outgoing Rep. Nancy Mace (R–S.C.) talk about the Lindsay Clancy case, the WNBA, and Sharia law on her show, Get Maced. The tatted congresswoman launched her podcast back in August on YouTube, and she has over 100,000 subscribers. 

And if none of these podcasts sound appealing to you, you are not alone. As Reason's Robby Soave pointed out in April after Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. launched his own pod, "There are just too many podcasts." 

It makes sense why so many politicians are hopping behind the mic. The 2024 election has been called "the podcast election," as both Donald Trump and Kamala Harris went on podcasts with large audiences to win support (obviously with varying degrees of success). And in 2025, when establishment Democrats realized they were losing their grip on the podcasting world, they desperately set out on a quixotic quest to find the "Joe Rogan of the left" to win back voters. That same summer, former Democratic National Committee chair Jaime Harrison even launched a podcast called At Our Table in a pathetic attempt to rebrand the Democratic Party. (In case you were wondering, his last episode has just cracked 100 views on YouTube). And political operatives know the power of podcasts is not going away. During the 2026 midterms, successful congressional candidates "made nearly three times as many podcast appearances as their losing opponents, according to Spotify data," reported Axios. 

The democratization of the media via podcasting or platforms like Substack is a good thing, as major networks no longer control political narratives. But if politicians only appear on podcasts with politically aligned hosts or launch their own shows, they can evade tough questions while appearing transparent. And, as Soave noted in April, we may occasionally need our leaders to step away from the podcasting set to do their taxpayer-funded jobs. 

Maybe the podcast market will soon be oversaturated, if it isn't already, and most of these podcasts will go the way of At Our Table. Not everyone has the podcasting magic in them. Plus, boring politicians will have to compete with hypnotizing AI fruit videos for the masses' attention. To win over 2028 voters, politicians may have to start thinking more about policies that will improve constituents' lives and less about their next MrBeast-style thumbnail.
news.summary: Everyone wants to be a podcaster. Politicians are no different.
news.author: Meagan O'Rourke,Reem Ibrahim

news.title: In new memoir, Biden accuses Netanyahu of putting political survival ahead of Israel
news.text: Former U.S. President Joe Biden takes aim at Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in his new memoir, accusing him of making promises he never intended to keep, repeatedly ignoring Washington's demands to reduce civilian casualties in Gaza and putting his own political interests ahead of Israel's long-term future. In excerpts from Promise Me, America published Friday by CNN, Biden describes his growing frustration with a leader he had known for decades, offering a bleak account of relations between the White House and Netanyahu's office during the war. “I had been calling on Israel to take precautions to reduce civilian suffering since the beginning of the conflict,” Biden writes. He says he raised those concerns repeatedly in private conversations with Netanyahu, who acknowledged that the growing Palestinian death toll was damaging Israel's international image and weakening American support for the war. Yet according to Biden, a familiar pattern emerged: Netanyahu would promise to do more, only for another Israeli military operation to result in further civilian deaths. “When we called them on it, the Israelis always had an explanation or excuse, but the result was the same,” Biden writes. His sharpest accusation is directed personally at the Israeli prime minister: “Bibi had no qualms about making promises he had no power — or intention — to keep.” Biden, whose relationship with Netanyahu dates back to his years in the Senate, describes how his patience gradually wore thin. He says he understood the extraordinary pressure Netanyahu faced following the October 7 Hamas massacre but could not accept his priorities. “While I understood that he was working under severe pressures, I was frustrated by his failure to think like a statesman and safeguard Israel’s long-term interests, not just his own short-term political needs,” Biden writes. The criticism is particularly striking given the attacks Biden faced in the United States throughout the war, with critics arguing that Netanyahu had repeatedly outmaneuvered him and secured extensive American military and diplomatic support despite ignoring White House demands. Biden rejects the suggestion that he was deceived, insisting that he made his position clear to Netanyahu time and again. The published excerpts, however, leave unanswered why he continued supporting Israel even after concluding that its prime minister was failing to honor his commitments. A series of confrontations The tensions between Biden and Netanyahu have already featured prominently in books by former senior administration officials. Brett McGurk, one of Biden's closest Middle East advisers and a central figure in negotiations to free Israeli hostages, described an especially heated telephone conversation in April 2024 in his book Brink, published last month. The confrontation followed an Israeli strike that killed seven World Central Kitchen aid workers in Gaza. According to McGurk, Biden angrily confronted Netanyahu over the attack and threatened to suspend American weapons supplies. In one exchange, he demanded to know what Netanyahu was doing and warned him that U.S. military assistance could not be taken for granted. “You think I'm Santa Claus? No Santa in Israel, pal,” McGurk quoted Biden as saying. McGurk recounted how close the administration came to taking extraordinary measures against Israel, including suspending weapons shipments. But U.S. intelligence warned of an unprecedented Iranian attack on Israel, forcing the White House to shift its attention toward preparing for the country's defense. According to McGurk, the administration would likely have taken significant steps against Israel had the Iranian threat not intervened. Major disagreements also emerged over negotiations to free the hostages held by Hamas. McGurk recalled a meeting with Netanyahu in early 2024 during which the prime minister concentrated on military operations and showed little urgency about discussing a hostage agreement. Nevertheless, McGurk places primary responsibility for the prolonged negotiating impasse on Hamas. He also argues that the Biden administration's public pressure on Israel sometimes encouraged the terrorist group to harden its negotiating position. Phil Gordon, who served as national security adviser to Vice President Kamala Harris, offered a different account last month. He argued that Netanyahu introduced new conditions into the hostage negotiations in July 2024, despite opposition from senior Israeli defense officials, delaying an agreement by approximately six months. The demands included maintaining Israeli troops along the Philadelphi Corridor, on the Gaza-Egypt border, and establishing a mechanism to monitor Palestinians returning to northern Gaza. Gordon said the delay came at a devastating cost, with thousands more Palestinians killed and additional Israeli hostages dying in captivity, including six murdered by Hamas in August 2024. Biden's criticism echoes accusations made by Harris in her memoir 107 Days, published last year. Harris described Netanyahu as dismissive toward her and argued that he preferred Donald Trump's return to the White House, believing the Republican president would be more receptive to his plans for Gaza. She also recalled a tense meeting in July 2024, during which she confronted Netanyahu about the humanitarian crisis and came away believing he was deliberately playing for time. But Harris also criticized Biden. In her account, the president struggled to express the same degree of empathy for Palestinian suffering that he showed toward Israeli and Ukrainian civilians. Biden now presents his own version of events, emphasizing how persistently he pressed Netanyahu to reduce civilian casualties and how frustrated he became when those demands failed to produce meaningful changes. The Gaza war also became a major source of opposition to Biden within the Democratic Party during the 2024 presidential campaign. The Uncommitted movement, which urged Democratic primary voters to withhold support from the president, gained traction in Michigan and Minnesota, states with significant Arab and Muslim communities. Biden nevertheless argues in his memoir that the primaries offered no clear warning of a collapse in his political standing. “The primaries sent no warning signs that I was in trouble,” he writes, maintaining that prominent Democrats avoided challenging him because they believed he remained too strong to defeat. Biden also invokes the October 7 attacks in defending himself against allegations of declining mental fitness. He challenges former special counsel Robert Hur, who described him in a February 2024 report as an elderly man with a poor memory. Biden notes that Hur interviewed him on October 8 and 9, 2023, immediately after Hamas' attack on Israel, when he was dealing with one of the most serious international crises of his presidency. “I had been up all night dealing with the aftershocks of a profound change to the global order,” Biden writes. “Go ask the Israeli leadership if they thought they were dealing with a diminished president that day.” He also points to his address to the nation and his visit to Israel 11 days after the interviews began, arguing that both demonstrated his ability to perform the duties of the presidency. Biden takes aim at Democrats and Trump But Biden reserves some of his harshest criticism, alongside his attacks on Netanyahu, for senior members of his own party. In a chapter examining his withdrawal from the 2024 presidential race, he describes feeling betrayed by longtime friends and political allies, particularly former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi and Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer. Biden recalls Pelosi telling him privately that no available poll showed he could defeat Trump. Schumer, meanwhile, visited his vacation home in Delaware to urge him to withdraw. “I told Schumer he had a lot of gumption (I may have said it differently at the time), coming to my home and telling me to get out of the race. Loyalty matters to me,” Biden writes. He also rejects the suggestion that he was unaware of the mounting pressure from Democratic lawmakers and governors who wanted him to withdraw. “I followed it. Hell, I was living it,” he writes, emphasizing that he knew exactly how many members of his party had withdrawn their support. “I wasn't living in a dream world,” he insists. Biden also disputes claims that he failed to understand the damage caused by his disastrous televised debate with Trump in June 2024. He acknowledges that his performance was poor but argues that other presidents had recovered from similarly disappointing debates and that he expected an opportunity to redeem himself in a second encounter. He recalls telling his wife, Jill, immediately after leaving the stage that he had badly messed up, although he admits using considerably stronger language. Biden and Pelosi, whose friendship had lasted decades, did not speak for months after he announced his withdrawal from the race. Trump, meanwhile, receives an unexpectedly different portrayal. Biden recounts their meeting at the White House following Trump's victory in November 2024, describing his longtime political rival as almost excessively flattering. According to the memoir, Trump told him, “You know, Joe, if it weren't for politics, I believe we'd be good friends.” Trump also reportedly expressed relief that he had not been forced to face Biden in the election. Biden attempted to brief his successor on major international challenges, including the wars in Ukraine and Gaza and relations with China, but says Trump appeared more interested in the personalities of foreign leaders than in the policy issues themselves. A meeting scheduled to last 30 minutes stretched to nearly two hours. The 480-page memoir is scheduled for publication on Tuesday, November 17. Biden, now 83, is undergoing treatment for advanced prostate cancer that has spread to his bones and announced this week that he would scale back appearances to promote the book. In an interview with People magazine published Wednesday, he said he would not have pursued another presidential term had he known about his illness while in office. He argued that running for the presidency at 80 while battling cancer would not have been the right decision.
news.summary: Former US president says repeated promises to curb civilian deaths in Gaza went unfulfilled, while Israeli officials always had ‘an explanation or excuse’; he also lashes out at Pelosi and Schumer for pressuring him to abandon his 2024 reelection campaign
news.author: Daniel Edelson, New York

news.title: Turns out Gen Z isn’t so conservative after all
news.text:
In the 2024 election, young voters, particularly young men, supported the GOP and President Donald Trump at shockingly high rates, raising the question of whether Generation Z possessed surprisingly conservative tendencies in the wake of the liberal millennial generation. But in 2026, young voters swung back toward the Democratic Party in droves — and played a key role in flipping Republican Senate seats in battleground states.

The narrative that Gen Z is quietly MAGA-friendly has crumbled. But that doesn’t mean Democrats have locked them in. The reality is that this cohort probably remains up for grabs by both parties.

Tufts University’s Center for Information & Research on Civic Learning and Engagement analyzed preliminary voter data and found that an estimated 66% of voters under 30 backed Democratic House candidates last week, while 31% voted for Republicans. That’s a much bigger margin than in 2024, when young voters broke for Democrats 56% to 42%.

Young voters were a key part of the coalition that flipped several Senate seats from red to blue. 

The difference is especially stark when you look at how young men went from favoring Trump to rebuking him. As John Della Volpe, the director of polling at the Harvard Kennedy School Institute of Politics, recently pointed out, preliminary New York Times data shows that men under 30 backed House Democrats 62% to 36%. Back in 2024, they preferred Trump over Democratic presidential candidate Kamala Harris 55% to 41%.

“No group switched more than young men in the entire electorate,” Della Volpe said on Monday during an appearance on MS NOW’s “Morning Joe.”

Notably, it seems to hold true at different levels of education — a crucial predictor of party affiliation in politics today. “Younger men without a college degree are about as likely to support Democrats as young men with a college degree,” he said.

Young voters were a key part of the coalition that flipped several Senate seats from red to blue. In Mississippi — where Scott Colom won by a razor-thin margin, an astonishing 76% of voters under 30 voted for him. As Stanford University political scientist Adam Bonica observed on Bluesky, the states where Senate seats changed party control, including North Carolina, Texas, South Carolina and Ohio, notably all showed under 30 voters breaking for Democratic candidates at a considerably higher rate (62% or higher) than the reliably blue state of Oregon (55%). In an election that showed the most comprehensive disapproval of an incumbent party in half a century, young voters in areas previously open to or friendly to Trump voiced their rejection of his second term loudly.

There were signs of this swing bubbling up before Election Day. As Vox’s Andrew Prokop reported ahead of the election, “The swings — and the feelings of betrayal and disappointment among prior Trump supporters — have been particularly dramatic among the young.” He pointed to a Pew Research poll released in October that found that “of people aged 19–34 who voted for Trump over Kamala Harris, only 49% approve of his job performance as president,” while noting, “In contrast, among Trump 2024 voters aged 50 and above, about 75% still approve of him.”

Tina Tang, who conducts focus groups for the Democratic-aligned firm Navigator Research, told Vox that many of those “Trump regretters” were disappointed with Trump’s broken promises on the economy. “[O]ne of the biggest frustrations we heard from young voters this time around: frustration with the job market,” Tang said. “We hear a lot about how he promised a lot of things; he promised the economy was going to get better, that costs were going to come down, that there would be more jobs.”

The history of polling numbers suggests that 2024 might have been more of an aberration for Gen Z, insofar as voters under 30 seem to be returning to a pronounced preference for Democrats that appeared in polling back in 2022 and 2023.

But the more prudent position might be to wait and see what happens in 2028 and beyond before coming to any definitive conclusions about their long-term leanings. After all, Gen Z is disproportionately likely to identify as independent compared to previous generational cohorts at the same age. They’ve come of age at a time of extraordinary mistrust in the political system. They’ve seen the electorate choose between unpopular presidential candidates who only narrowly prevailed over one another for the past decade. They’ve watched both parties talk about addressing the cost-of-living crisis — while failing to effectively tackle it. It’s not surprising that many of them still seem to lack convictions about where to place their trust.

But one thing appears clear: Whoever can persuade them — and then deliver — on promises to substantially improve economic prospects for working people has the best chance of locking this crucial voting bloc into their party.
news.author: Kaivan Shroff

news.title: How One Freshman Photo Defines the New Congress
news.text: Five newly elected lawmakers posed for photograph on the steps of the U.S. Capitol this week. Together, they offer a snapshot of the political forces shaping America after the 2026 midterms. From a 29-year-old democratic socialist to a 78-year-old Trump-aligned conservative, the five represent some of the generational, ideological and geographic differences that could shape the House of Representatives when the new Congress convenes in January. The image, taken on November 12 during freshman orientation, shows Melat Kiros, the first Black woman elected to Congress from Colorado; former Maine Governor Paul LePage; Denise Powell, who flipped Nebraska's competitive 2nd Congressional District; Jeremy Moss, the first openly gay person elected to Congress from Michigan; and Robert White, who will succeed Eleanor Holmes Norton as Washington, D.C.'s non-voting delegate. Newsweek contacted representatives for Kiros, LePage, Powell, Moss and White for comment by email. They were among more than 100 incoming House members attending orientation and they reflect some of the competing priorities facing the next Congress: a Democratic Party balancing its progressive ambitions with the demands of winning competitive districts, Republicans confronting their future after electoral defeat, and continuing battles over political representation and federal power. Melat Kiros – The Gen Z Socialist The 29-year-old first-time candidate delivered an upset in July when she beat Democratic Colorado Representative Diana DeGette in the primary. Kiros is among a new generation of democratic socialists challenging established figures within the Democratic Party, following the political rise of New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani. Kiros has promised to fight what she describes as the oligarchy, oppose President Donald Trump, abolish U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and pass Medicare for All. She made her criticism of U.S. support for Israel central to her primary campaign. While that message clearly resonated with voters in her district, it could lead to clashes with some of her more moderate new colleagues in the Democratic Party. Her arrival in Washington raises a question for Democrats following their midterm victories: how far can the party move to the left while maintaining the broader coalition that brought it back to power? Paul LePage – The Conservative Counterweight At 78, LePage represents a very different generation and political ideology from Kiros. He won in Maine’s 2nd District, which Trump carried by almost 10 points in the 2024 presidential race and which is by far the more Republican-leaning of the state's two districts. A businessman before entering politics, LePage served two terms as Maine's governor from 2011 to 2019. He lost his bid to return to office in 2022 to Democratic Governor Janet Mills. LePage has a history of provocative remarks. In 2016, he described himself as "Donald Trump before Donald Trump became popular." During his 2010 gubernatorial campaign, he said he would tell then-President Barack Obama to "go to hell." In 2011, amid a dispute over his attendance at Martin Luther King Jr. events, he told the NAACP to "kiss my butt." His election puts a Trump-aligned and oft-combative conservative into a political region now dominated by Democrats, and will represent the GOP as it seeks to redefine itself following its midterm defeat and ahead of the 2028 presidential election. LePage's victory illustrates the political divide within Maine, a state that has favored Democrats in presidential elections but where rural and working-class voters have remained receptive to Trump. Moderate Democrat Jared Golden managed to bridge that divide, repeatedly winning reelection in a district that backed the Republican president. His departure, and the Democrats' failure to retain the seat, raise questions about whether the party can compete in such territory without candidates who share Golden's more centrist approach. Denise Powell – The Swing District Winner While Kiros and LePage represent different ends of the political spectrum, Powell's victory illustrates the importance of winning voters in competitive territory. Powell defeated Republican Brinker Harding to win Nebraska's 2nd Congressional District, becoming the first woman elected to represent the district and the first Latina elected to Congress from the state. The Omaha-based district is one of the country's most competitive House seats and typically draws national attention from both parties. Nebraska has voted Republican in every statewide presidential election since 1968, including Trump's three campaigns. But the Omaha-based 2nd Congressional District has always been a bit bluer, backing Vice President Kamala Harris in 2024 while electing a Republican to the House. Powell, who co-founded a group that coached local women on how to run for office, demonstrated how Democrats can make gains in politically mixed territory. Her victory also highlights a challenge for the party as it prepares to govern. While progressive candidates such as Kiros have found success challenging the Democratic establishment from the left, Powell's win illustrates the importance of appealing to voters in districts where neither party can take victory for granted. Her success may provide Democrats with a case study in how to compete in areas where suburban, urban and rural interests intersect, particularly as the party looks toward the 2028 elections. Jeremy Moss - The Michigan History Maker Moss, who won Michigan's 11th Congressional District, represents another strand of Democratic politics as the party considers its direction following the midterms. The Democrat will succeed Representative Haley Stevens in January, becoming the first openly gay person elected to Congress from Michigan. Moss has served in the Michigan State Legislature since 2015 and ran his congressional campaign on tackling the cost of living, while putting his support behind a "robust public option" to achieve universal healthcare coverage. During his campaign, Moss sought to shift attention from culture-war disputes to economic concerns, while defending transgender rights. In an October interview with The Advocate, he argued that transgender athletes were not responsible for rising living costs or barriers to affordable healthcare. His win comes as the Great Lakes State’s Senate race was bitter and closely watched, after a high-profile rift in Michigan Democratic politics, when Stevens—who lost the Democratic Senate primary to Abdul El-Sayed—endorsed Republican Senate nominee Mike Rogers just days before the general election. As the Democrats define their agenda moving ahead, Moss has been clear that the party needs to be “stronger, bolder, tougher,” per an October interview with The Advocate. One challenge for Democrats moving forward will be whether internal disputes over strategy and identity politics distract from advancing their legislative agenda. Robert White - The D.C. Delegate Of the five lawmakers pictured, White is the only one who will not have a vote on final legislation in the House. The successor to Norton will represent the nation's capital in Congress without the same voting powers as his four fellow freshmen. His election comes amid continuing disputes over the district's autonomy and the federal government's involvement in city affairs under the Trump administration. White campaigned on defending the district against federal interference, with disputes ranging from the embattled Lincoln Reflecting Pool renovation to the contested renovation of the East Potomac Golf Links. “Together, we will fight Trump and his allies in Congress as they attempt to use D.C. as a testing ground for their radical right-wing agenda,” White says on his campaign website. He has pledged to build on Norton's decades-long campaign for Washington, D.C., statehood and full voting representation, while defending the district against federal interference. With Democrats set to control both chambers of Congress, he hopes to persuade lawmakers to make statehood a legislative priority. His position highlights another political divide that will continue into the new Congress: the question of who gets a full voice in the federal government and how much control the White House should exercise over the nation's capital. For a moment on the Capitol steps, the five incoming lawmakers stood together for a photograph. When Congress convenes in January, they will bring different political priorities, constituencies and visions for the country's future. Four of the five lawmakers pictured are Democrats, but their different political priorities illustrate the challenges facing a party preparing to govern. From democratic socialism to swing-district pragmatism and the fight for D.C. statehood, their competing ambitions offer a glimpse of the debates that could define the next Congress. Newsweek’s reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story. Learn more about Martyn here. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Daniel Orton and Rhian Morgan.
news.summary: One photo of five incoming lawmakers captures the political divisions and competing priorities shaping the next Congress.
news.author: Marni Rose McFall

news.title: Mississippi Goddam: Scott Colom Is the Answer to Anyone Who Looked Down on the South
news.text:
This is what an older Black woman said to MS NOW’s Nnamdi Egwuonwu as he interviewed Scott Colom supporters on the Tougaloo College campus Thursday night. The crowd was waiting for Colom to speak after his historic victory, becoming the first Black Mississippian elected to statewide office since Reconstruction, and its first Democratic senator in nearly a half century. The woman did not give her name, but her simple statement has tattooed itself inside my brain.
“To understand the world, you must first understand a place like Mississippi” is a more famous cautionary quip that scratches at the same sentiment. If you’ve known anyone from Mississippi, you’ve probably heard it. Everyone cites William Faulkner, even though nobody has definitively sourced it. But as the world looks with fresh eyes on my home state, the wisdom checks out.
Onlookers, including longtime national political strategists, seem surprised by Colom’s win. Mississippians are not. The extremes of the moral universe have always been duking it out down there, which makes Mississippi not strange or anomalous, but illustrative.
There’s no avoiding the facts: Human beings have committed the most brutal violence imaginable against their fellow humans in Mississippi, as a matter of law and legacy. One of the consequences of that horror is that it has become prophecy. It is impossible not to feel a sense—from within the state and from without—of frustration and dread that it is taking way too long to emerge from a racism that has raptured the entire culture.
But to people who do not know Mississippians, who do not understand Mississippi—to those who suggest any right-minded or good people simply up and leave, or think the rest of the country should abandon all hope, or worse, look away entirely—you are missing one of the most important threads in the future of American politics and culture. Colom got at this rub when he said that outlets like Cook Political Report, who prognosticate a “solid R” conclusion, are destructive. “They made it much more difficult to fundraise and are part of the reason the South has been neglected for so long,” he wrote. And if you dismiss possibility in Mississippi, you are compounding the neglect. You are part of the destruction.
Mississippi is not who you think we are.
During the race, he drew national attention not only for his prospect of flipping the unflippable, but also because he was doing so through one of the most vivid, creatively engaged, and original campaigns in modern politics. He built a coalition virally, with his twin brother Andrew Robert Colom as collaborator, offering “Sheeeeit” to the world (yes, that’s how many white Mississippians really talk), along with a Hollywood-worthy Sinners send-up, and Andrew’s searing spoken-word poem set to the strains of Fannie Lou Hamer. Colom even stood in line at a Trump rally to speak earnestly with voters who would otherwise be against him—I guarantee he won some of them over.
His entire strategy was built on making people recognize Mississippi, in all its underdog idiosyncrasies. He asked Kamala Harris to campaign with him, even as many in his party advised him it would be an error, because he knew she would draw media attention to underfunded hospitals. And he took the phone call informing him that he’d won while wearing a Richard Pryor hoodie. Because we like to laugh in Mississippi, okay?
As Kiese Laymon, novelist, memoirist and modern-day Mississippi bard, told me, “Once I saw the protein ad, I knew he’d win.”
History doesn't echo in Mississippi, it rhymes. You can draw a straight line from the murders of Medgar Evers, or those of James Chaney, Andrew Goodman, and Michael Schwerner, to the killings of Jorge Gomez or Renee Good or Alex Pretti. You can draw a straight line from Theodore Bilbo to Tate Reeves to Donald Trump.
As Kiese wrote in this magazine in 2020, Mississippi politics flow from its culture. (Incidentally, Kiese and Colom both attended Millsaps College, about 10 years apart, and had the same thesis adviser.) In Mississippi: A Poem, In Days, Kiese describes how he got into “an altercation with two fraternities on Bid Day"—when the students who want to be in the Greek system receive offers from frat and sorority houses—"Some fraternity members wore Confederate capes, Afro wigs, and others blackened their faces.” They called Kiese and his girlfriend the n-word.
I have never written about the heartbreak of seeing the future governor of Mississippi in that group of white boys, proudly representing the Kappa Alpha fraternity and its confederate commitment to Black suffering. I have never admitted that after playing basketball against Tate all through high school, and knowing that he went to a public school called Florence, not a segregation academy, like so many other white boys we knew, it hurt my feelings to see Tate doing what white boys who pledged their identities to the Old South ideologies were supposed to do.
When I saw Tate in that confederate cacophony of drunken white boyhood, doing what they did, I knew he could one day be governor of Mississippi and president of the United States.
That is still the most damning thing I can ever say about a white boy from Mississippi.
Damning things still happen, and will again. Just days ago, as the votes continued to stack up for Colom, the old ugliness reared its head. White women in my hometown, students at the University of Mississippi, were captured on video making racist gestures—gesturing and making sounds like monkeys—at their Black neighbor’s video doorbell. The school, still embarrassingly insistent on calling itself “Ole Miss,” continues to investigate, while the offenders get so much more grace than they deserve from the victims and their families, as you can see in their CBS interview. I feel deep shame in these moments, because I know this is what so many people think Mississippi is. There is no excuse for it, and no explanation beyond the obvious. The shame should be obvious, too, but a white person from Mississippi is compelled to express it.
The women are not from Mississippi, according to a source familiar; one, Alaina Kunes, is from Wisconsin, where a car dealership that bears her family’s name is now being sued for a separate allegation of racist actions. This is not an excuse, but rather a fear: that Mississippi’s reputation for the worst parts of history continues to attract the worst sorts of people.
But this is partly what Faulkner, or whoever it was, meant by understanding the world through the lens of Mississippi: everywhere, we must hope our better angels prevail.
Local private schools, as I understood them, were inherently racist. Public school was a choice of one, and I got a world-class education in the Oxford school system. (Hyde-Smith attended Lawrence County Academy and she sent her own child to Brookhaven Academy, both segregation academies.) My class of 2000—I came up with the same kids from kindergarten through high school—was roughly half Black and half white, with the skinniest pie slivers of anything else. I left for college and never moved back, but my parents, brother, and extended family are still there. Today, Mississippi’s public-school students are doing better than most of their peers across the nation; my own children in the New York City school system are getting a more segregated, less excellent education than I did.
My father, a green-energy mayor and a Barack Obama appointee to the Tennessee Valley Authority (fired by Trump amid a Republican board takeover), pushed throughout my childhood to take the confederate flag off the state flag and to remove the confederate monument that still mars the Oxford Square. I was about 8 years old when someone keyed “LIBERALS” into the trunk of our Honda Civic, probably because of the RAY MABUS FOR GOVERNOR bumper sticker. I recall being worried about it, until I saw that my parents were amused.
As white Southern liberals, we were in a tiny minority. And though the mantle was worn proudly, it was more existential than that—you were proud to be a Democrat not because it was one party over another, but because it was a stand-in for compassion, common good, and humanity. And nowhere could this be truer, or more necessary, than in Mississippi. (By way of disclosure, I see no conflicts in telling you all this. As former TIME editor Rick Stengel says, “you should be non-partisan, but not neutral. Journalists must be biased in favor of the truth and facts. Biased in favor of democracy itself.” And this is the truth, in favor of democracy.)
Scott Colom and I were born a year apart in the earliest 1980s, during a sort of second-wave new-New South rebranding. More jobs were coming into the state thanks to manufacturing, more national attention was being paid to Black Mississippians’ cultural contributions (the Delta Blues Museum opened in 1979). William Winter was governor the years of our respective births, and he gave us free kindergarten. William Allain, whose moment was virtually destroyed by a racist, homophobic GOP slander campaign, followed. And Allain was succeeded by Mabus—who won on the slogan “Mississippi will never be last again.” Now, with the exception of Ronnie Musgrove, the governor has been a Republican since 1992. We’ve never had a Black person, or a woman for that matter. Have you had many good thoughts about Mississippi in all this time? I don’t think you have.
Heavy, Kiese’s devastating and raw memoir of coming of age as a Black boy in Mississippi, written in address to his activist and educator mother, gives his own view into 1980s and 90s Mississippi: “You worked on Governor Mabus’s campaign and kept talking about how much was possible politically in Mississippi because it was the blackest state in the nation,” he writes. And his mother says to him: “Do you understand what’s possible if we actually get effective radical politicians in place down here?” Kiese responds, ”I’m glad Mabus won but hearing about it every day is just kinda mee-guh.” Meager. It was not enough then, and we have plenty far to go.
Heavy was published in October 2018, just before Stacey Abrams turned Georgia purple, signaling to the rest of the country that it was time to take notice of the deeply disenfranchised Southern states.
When I reached out to Mabus, who went on to become Bill Clinton’s ambassador to Saudi Arabia and then Obama’s Secretary of the Navy, he identified the dominoes that knocked towards Colom’s win: the Supreme Court's gutting of the Voting Rights Act, rampant corruption, a welfare scandal featuring Brett Favre, and “office holders taking constituents for granted over decades.” Mabus was a young man working for Winter when Colom and I were little, and this election, he said, “brings hope for the future.”
It doesn’t really matter which party you’d like to claim. Repulsive policies will eventually push everyone away. Mississippi Republicans are not moderate, are not descended of gentle governance. (See: Bilbo et al.) This is the state that put “personhood” on the ballot as part of a national anti-abortion strategy; fortunately for all y’all, Mississippians rejected the idea of life beginning at conception. Lynn Fitch, the current attorney general, not only effortfully attempted to overturn the results of the 2020 presidential election, but she is the signed counsel for the petitioners in the Dobbs brief, which ultimately reversed Roe v Wade. (Because I keep underscoring to you the infinite refractions of Mississippi, Fitch also went after Colom for one of his ads that used AI; he removed it.) Even the affidavit ballots that have taken so long to count are a result of strident, generational attempts by Republicans to disenfranchise Black voters. Which is why Mississippians knew, as the Colom-Hyde Smith race came down to those affidavits, exactly in whose favor they would tally up. Were it not for the dedication of young Black canvassers—especially Black women—and homegrown mobilization efforts, things would have gone differently.
“There is a radical history of Black academics, activists, lawyers and judges who have really been working to see a Mississippi where this was possible,” Kiese emailed me over the weekend. “I am thankful that someone like Leslie McLemore who was a young member of Hamer's Mississippi Democratic Party can see what they worked and died for.”
What does Colom’s win mean for Kiese? “It means that the people, not any party, get what they organize and fight for,” he replied. “Our state taught the world that again last week.”
After Trump won in 2024, an old childhood friend who’d gone MAGA texted me a GIF of a penis ejaculating stars that reconstituted in the shape of a patriotic eagle. Flash forward a year later, he's angry about gas prices, and, more striking to me, horrified by the war in Gaza. Colom’s protein ad is for him, and that nerve of enthusiasm it struck is going to keep firing.
Colom didn’t run on pronouns or any numerical strain of woke. He has said he is a fan of Trump’s border security, agrees with him on certain tax policies, and supports the Second Amendment. When asked about improving wages for government employees, he has said he wants to take care of teachers—and cops. As Colom told Jen Psaki in a televised interview, “We gotta be a party that represents our whole country, that understands all parts of the country.”
Now that people outside Mississippi are waking up to Colom, leftists may find his centrism irritating or even offensive. You may find a new reason to look down your noses at Mississippi. It all but promises to provide an opportunity.
So I will just leave you with the brothers Colom.
The poetry of Andrew:
“They lied about Mississippi. Said that evil lived in one state, but the cotton cow fed the nation. Europe eating off the same plate. They lied about Mississippi. Said the torture was only here, but the banker’s desk in northern mills still dripping blood from hostage tears. They lied to us all. That’s propaganda machine on both sides, running on slander…. Denying the nation condoned it, denying the nation owned it, denying the nation fed off pain… They lied about Mississippi. Said that evil lived in one state.”
He says, invoking Hamer, “Mississippi Freedom Party began again.”
And the vision of Scott: “There is nothing wrong with Mississippi that can’t be fixed by what’s right.”
news.summary: To those who doubt the power and potential of Mississippi, please reconsider. To the good people there, keep the faith.
news.author: Claire Howorth

news.title: WATCH: This Scott Colom Protein Ad was More Popular Than His Obama Endorsement
news.text:
After a nail-biting race decided by only a few thousand votes, Scott Colom was declared Mississippi’s first Black senator-elect in 145 years. “One of the best political ads ever,” an unconventional campaign advertisement about protein, helped him secure his historic victory.

The 30-second clip tees off a television interview featuring Colom’s opponent, Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, who was running for reelection, in which she responded to concerns about rising beef prices by saying there are “so many proteins to choose from.”

“Pick another protein? Shiiiid, I’d rather pick another senator instead,” one man says in the ad before flipping a beef patty on a grill.

“Pick another protein?” a woman says while enjoying a plate at a restaurant. “She done lost her damn mind. I’d rather pick another senator.”

Another woman at a grocery store freezer aisle nearly drops the f-bomb in response to being told to “pick another protein” when Colom appears on the screen, chuckling. “Pick another senator instead,” he says.

The video from last month, which has over 3.9 million views on TikTok, has been called the “coldest campaign ad ever” by online commenters. Its simple, straightforward messaging, and the rejection of Hyde-Smith’s “let them eat cake”-type statement stuck in the minds of Mississippians, so much so that “pick another senator” caught the attention of people across the country during midterm elections.

The ad even outperformed a video released a day earlier of former President Barack Obama encouraging Mississippi voters to vote for Colom. The senator-elect also received endorsements from Kamala Harris, Chuck Schumer, Raphael Warnock, Elizabeth Warren, Pete Buttigieg and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, among others.

Last week, Colom gave kudos for the ad to two Black men: Patrick Gaspard, a former Obama administration diplomat who came up with the idea to “do something edgy” with Hyde-Smith’s “inexcusable gaffe,” and Ryan Sayles, a 27-year-old content creator from Mississippi who directed and edited the popular clip: “He should be considered the breakout-star of this cycle. He’s going to be a giant in the media consultant game. He did GAME CHANGING work with SO little.”

Now, Sayles has become one to watch. A mass communications alum of Alcorn State University, according to the Washington Post, he had never been involved with political campaigns before working with Colom. He was first brought on to the senator-elect’s campaign as a photographer for an event in October and did such a great job that the team wanted to continue working with him, Sayles told Politico.

District Attorney Colom prevailed over incumbent Mississippi Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith. His win, which was called Wednesday after counties verified outstanding ballots, makes him the state’s first Black senator since 1881, during the Reconstruction era, and the state’s first Democratic senator in 44 years.

It follows a blue wave that swept through the South, including Georgia electing Keisha Lance Bottoms as the nation’s first Black woman governor, and several historic wins for Black candidates across the country during this month’s midterm elections, in part due to high Black voter turnout. Nearly 40 percent of Mississippians and over 130,000 voters in the state are Black.
news.summary:
"Pick another protein? I'd rather pick another senator," Mississippians said in Scott Colum's viral campaign ad.

news.title: Vance and Kamala top presidential race for 2028 — but surprising candidates come in second place
news.text:
The latest polling after the stunning midterm Republican massacre shows that second-place candidates in the presidential race for 2028 are making gains on the top contenders.

An Economist/YouGov poll showed failed presidential candidate Kamala Harris at the top for the Democratic nomination and Vice President JD Vance heading up the Republicans.

Harris has a positive favorability rating of only 41%, while 50% said they have an unfavorable opinion of Harris.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio came in second place for Republicans with 33% to Vance's 40%. Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis finished third with 14%.

The field is far more crowded for the Democrats. Harris took the top spot with only 20% of support, and Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff of Georgia received 15%.

Only three other Democrats — outgoing California Gov. Gavin Newsom, Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York, and Pete Buttigieg — received at least 10%.

Harris isn't terribly popular overall, however. She has a positive favorability rating of only 41%, while 50% said they have an unfavorable opinion of her.

Vance fares worse than Harris in terms of favorability. Only 35% say they have a favorable view of the vice president, while 52% said they have an unfavorable view of him.

Both Vance and Harris dropped in favorability from the same poll in October, where the vice president had 41% favorability and Harris had 43%.

Not surprisingly, President Donald Trump continues to poll lower after voters widely rejected Republicans in the midterm elections. Just 32% of respondents said they approve of the president's job performance while 63% said they disapprove.

RELATED: Social media mocks Kamala Harris after she announces book on doomed campaign

The poll also found that more than twice as many respondents opposed the president's plan to build a 250-foot United States Triumphal Arch in Washington, D.C. Only 22% said they favor the arch, and 57% said they oppose it.

The poll has a sample of 1,685 U.S. citizens and was taken between Monday and Wednesday. It has a margin of error of 3 percentage points.

news.title: The Millennial Politician Has Risen (To Your FYP)
news.text:
In his victory speech in the wee hours of the morning after Election Day, incoming Sen. James Talarico (D-Texas) shouted out the power of grassroots support in the face of mass spending. 

“All the money in the world is no match for the people of Texas,” Talarico said. “And we just sent a message to every billionaire megadonor, every trillionaire megadonor, every corrupt defender of this broken political system in this state, in this country: Power belongs to the people.”

Talarico’s team posted the speech to his TikTok account, which is followed by over 2 million people, where it sits at a cool 158,000 views. It’s an indicator of the other type of grassroots support that proved integral to his victory.

Several marquee candidates this cycle, like Talarico and fellow Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed (D-Mich.), were practically main characters on video-forward social media like TikTok and Instagram Reels, and associated surrogate accounts racked up millions of views on their behalf. 

They posted “Mean Girls” parodies comparing their opponent to Regina George and clapbacks to being accused of “low testosterone,” among short, snappy videos communicating their top priorities. (One, on El-Sayed team’s page, included those ideas in a reel showcasing his ‘Abdul Aura,’ borrowing from popular Gen Alpha slang.) Not to mention the dozens and dozens of edits of candidates up and down the ballot that have Made Democrats Sexy Again.

Parker Butler and Lauren Kapp, Gen Z strategists who founded the digital agency Luminary, say that campaigns are finally waking up to the truth of today’s politics: Hacking the attention economy is mission-critical to winning. 

“Organic attention, in particular, is the driving force of politics,” said Butler. Luminary worked on Talarico’s social campaign and was previously part of the team behind the in/famous 2024 KamalaHQ account. He suggested that other parts of the party hadn’t fully processed this notion at the start of the cycle and may have seen social strategy as a “side project for like the kids to post their fun memes or whatever.”

That idea “has been done away with, and it’s taken a while, I think, for a lot of party operatives to catch up to this fact,” said Butler. 

Texas’ Senate race was a prime example. Intermittent trillionaire Elon Musk spent a small fortune — $158 million of the nearly half a billion dollars he invested in the midterms overall — to back Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton’s U.S. Senate bid and smear Talarico in the process. While polling showed that Talarico’s unfavorables inched up with older demographics more prone to watching television ads, his favorables grew 16% from July to October with voters under 35, the group most likely to engage with his online virality, per Fox News polling.

Georgia Gov.-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms also beat a billionaire GOP challenger who significantly outpaced her in spending. And while her content was not as viral as Talarico’s — she sits at just under 150,000 followers — her team did have a presence on TikTok. (Her opponent’s account has less than 4,000 followers.)

“You see in so many of the marquee races of this past cycle, including Texas, where money did not make the difference,” said Butler. “You can’t just buy your way to victory anymore, and you have to be a lot more creative to break through.”

The more establishment-leaning wings of the party seem to have caught on, too. The Democratic National Committee’s official account, for instance, boasts over 7 million followers and has seen skyrocketing growth since the last presidential election, when Kamala’ Harris digital presence, KamalaHQ, developed a cult following. Per a DNC official, their accounts across TikTok, Facebook and YouTube have seen 501% growth in impressions since 2024 and a staggering 749% increase in engagement since then. Just this cycle, the DNC TikTok account gained 4.5 million followers, and within the past year, nearly two-thirds of its viewers (70%) were under 34. 

But believing this was simply the cycle of the “fan cam” video montage is a “limited” takeaway, Kapp said. It’s not just muscular candidates in tight T-shirts that drove engagement — candidates were able to effectively communicate their platform and priorities. 

“We’re entering this new era of talent within the Democratic Party, where you have millennials and younger folks that are coming into power that are scrolling in the same way that the three of us are, and that’s a very unique experience,” Kapp said. She believes much of the success of various candidate accounts can be attributed to heightened risk-taking and a rapid-response feel over manicured ads. “They’re able to show their personality, but also communicate their policy in a very genuine manner in comparison to the old guard,” Kapp said.

Candidates eyeing the White House in 2028 — as well as other Democratic Party stakeholders — are taking notice. Pete Buttigieg, Wes Moore, Gavin Newsom and Jon Ossoff all have accounts on TikTok. 

And while no one is arguing that traditional ads are a thing of the past, these accounts are resonating with parts of the potential electorate that may not have been paying attention otherwise. Per Butler and Kapp, in 2024, 77% of Kamala HQ’s content was viewed from TikTok’s For You Page, rather than from a profile search or from users’ feeds of accounts they already followed. Two years later, that figure has spiked, with nearly all their content, 91%, viewed through that For You Page. 

“This shows how the For You Page is increasingly the way people are viewing content online instead of from who they’re following. Organic social is becoming more like targeted ads,” said Butler.

Kapp added that compared to 2024, Democrats now have a more varied and competitive stream of amplifiers for their content and messages after Republicans long dominated the broader political influencer, podcaster and news aggregator space. (See: the manosphere.) El-Sayed’s campaign account, AbdulHQ, has over a million TikTok followers, as does Team Talarico’s Facebook page.

“These are huge assets for these incoming senators to have,” said Kapp. “The fact that they not only have large followings on their principal accounts, but have these surrogate accounts that they can rely on to amplify their messaging and create this ecosystem of accounts in order to uplift them online.” 

“Not everything makes sense to post on a principal account, and it’s really important to have these other accounts that are able to lift you,” she said.

news.title: Vance, Rubio, Ossoff and Buttigieg lead 2028 White House hopefuls
news.text:
Four potential contenders in the 2028 race for the White House have caught American voters’ attention with their early jockeying: Republicans JD Vance and Marco Rubio and Democrats Jon Ossoff and Pete ​Buttigieg, according to the latest Reuters/Ipsos poll.

None of the four has yet formally launched a campaign and the parties’ 2028 nominating contests are more than a year away, leaving plenty of time ‌for new contenders to emerge and for voters’ views to change.

The Misinformation Monitor newsletter rounds up international misinformation narratives, with a “Real or Fake?” quiz in every edition. Sign up here.

Some 45% of Republican voters polled said they believed Secretary of State Rubio would be an “excellent” presidential candidate, with 43% saying the same of Vice President Vance. Former Transportation Secretary Buttigieg and US Senator Ossoff, of Georgia, each got that rating from 29% of Democratic voters.

The poll, which surveyed 1,705 US adults nationwide including roughly 500 registered voters from each party and was completed on Monday, had a margin of error of 5 percentage points for Republican and Democratic ​voters.

President Donald Trump, struggling with an approval rating near the lowest of his career, looms large over the conversation for both parties. Republicans are divided on whether they want a candidate who breaks with Trump ​or follows in his footsteps, while Democrats, who are flying high after routing Republicans in the November 3 congressional elections, are divided on how aggressively to go after ⁠the president, such as through impeachment.

Trump has quizzed allies on whom they prefer Vance or Rubio and in a Sunday interview with CBS’s “60 Minutes” said he would “not necessarily” make an endorsement in the Republican primary.

‘MANAGED TO DO HIS ​JOB’

Barbara Rezner, an attorney in Florida who voted for Trump in the last three presidential elections, said she prefers Rubio over Vance, whom she considers too far to the right and too close to the president.

“Rubio has managed ​to do his job. He’s stayed off most people’s radar because he hasn’t done anything too far left, too far right, too crazy,” Rezner said.

The modest but growing dissatisfaction with Trump among Republicans is centered on the president’s decision to launch a war on Iran that has driven fuel prices higher. Rubio has been notably absent from many of the so-far fruitless peace talks with Iran despite being the nation’s top diplomat. Vance has shown signs of wanting to distance himself as well, saying publicly that the Republican drubbing ​in the midterm elections owed to the war with Iran.

A dozen-odd other Republicans are also in the national conversation over 2028 contenders, with Florida Governor Ron DeSantis among the best regarded, with 32% of Republicans rating him ​as an excellent option. Others – like Trump’s son, Donald Trump Jr., and Texas US Senator Ted Cruz – have their fans, but also many detractors.

[1/4]U.S. Vice President JD Vance President and Secretary of State Marco Rubio attend U.S. President Donald Trump’s address to the nation about election security, at the East Room of the White House in Washington, D.C., U.S., July 16, 2026. SAUL LOEB/Pool via REUTERS/File Photo Purchase Licensing Rights, opens new tab

OSSOFF AND BUTTIGIEG

Among Democrats, Ossoff is at the top of many voters’ lists, with 29% of the party’s registered ‌voters rating ⁠him as excellent. Ossoff has grabbed headlines in recent months by calling Trump corrupt and unfit for office in unusually direct language, and last week he won his re-election race by 18 percentage points in Georgia, a state Trump carried by 2 points in 2024.

Buttigieg also gets the excellent rating from 29% of Democrats. Buttigieg also ran for president in 2020 and is better known nationally than Ossoff.

About one in five Democrats say they have never heard of Buttigieg, compared to roughly one in three who say the same about Ossoff. Very few Republicans are unfamiliar with Vance, but about one in six said they do not know who Rubio is. For candidates in either party, starting ​the election cycle with more name recognition can save ​money that would be spent getting the candidate’s ⁠name out, but examples abound of little-known candidates catching fire during the campaign, as happened with former President Bill Clinton.

Buttigieg and Ossoff are considered moderates among Democrats, and that appeals to Democratic voters like Ed Blair, a retired pig farmer in southern Illinois, who gives Buttigieg a better rating in part because Ossoff is less familiar.

“I do favor ​the more moderate candidates over the more progressive ones,” said Blair, who is wary of proposed major shifts like expanding federal Medicare health insurance coverage from ​all seniors to everyone in the ⁠country. Blair would prefer gradual shifts, such as expanding Medicare to cover all children. “In going towards some of the progressive policies, small steps need to be taken rather than large ones to give people time to adapt.”

The Reuters/Ipsos poll shows other well-known moderates – like former Vice President Kamala Harris, who lost to Trump in the 2024 presidential election, and California Governor Gavin Newsom – each get “excellent candidate” ratings of 23%, higher than the 15% of Democrats who view progressive stalwart Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, ⁠a US representative ​for New York, that way.

Ocasio-Cortez told CNN after the midterms that impeaching Trump should be an option on the table, while Buttigieg told the New ​Yorker magazine he is “not very interested” in impeachment.

Elaine Kamarck, a Democratic strategist, cautioned against reading too deeply into the public’s current views this far out from the 2028 election. “It’s a world away,” Kamarck said. “There are lots of people in both parties who are still deciding if they ​are going to run. You might be able to predict who will run, but you certainly don’t know anything about who is going to be ahead.”
