news.title: Scott Colom’s U.S. Senate win changes the narrative about Mississippi
news.text:
As Martin Luther King Jr. listed the places he dreamed of freedom taking root, he put the word “even” before the state where I was born. There was wall-to-wall racism in the United States, and the whole bloc of Jim Crow states was notoriously deadly. But from the steps of the Lincoln Memorial in 1963, King spoke of a day when “even the state of Mississippi…will be transformed.”

Even. With that one word, King voiced what so many people believed, what so many people still believe, about Mississippi: that it is singularly oppressive, the last place a Black person in the U.S. would want to be.

With that one word, King voiced what so many people believed, what so many people still believe, about Mississippi: that it is singularly oppressive, the last place a Black person in the U.S. would want to be.

“Isn’t that where prejudice kinda started at?” a Black man, in Louisiana of all places, once asked when I said where I was from. A Black woman in Boston said she’d been proud she’d never stepped foot in my home state. But while in Memphis, she said, she impulsively crossed the bridge just to say she had. Joke’s on her, because the bridges out of Memphis lead to Arkansas, but the point is she considered Mississippi so frightening, she’d only stick a toe in.

Despite the state’s reputation as a thing unto itself — “They got white folks down there that scare white folks,” is how Richard Pryor put it — even Mississippi joined last week’s blue wave and voted to send Democrat Scott Colom to the U.S. Senate. Colom was finally able to claim victory Wednesday, more than a week after Election Day.

His win is historic in part because every Democrat the state previously sent to the Senate was some combination of slave owner, Confederate soldier or segregationist. But it’s even more historic because Colom is Black, and for the first time, voters in the Blackest state in the country have elected a Black person to a statewide office. (Republicans Hiram Revels and Blanche K. Bruce, Black U.S. senators from Mississippi’s Reconstruction era, were chosen by the state legislature, as senators were before the ratification of the 17th Amendment.)

Colom, a 43-year-old district attorney for four Northeast Mississippi counties, prevailed against the 67-year-old Republican incumbent Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, who eight years ago, infamously winked at the South’s history of lynching when she joked that if a certain supporter “invited me to a public hanging, I’d be on the front row.” That seeming fondness for the state’s racist past didn’t cost her then, and it may not have directly factored into her loss to Colom, but her initial refusal to apologize exposed her as an arrogant white Southern politician who couldn’t conceive of such offensiveness costing her. How could it — in Mississippi?

According to an MS NOW analysis, in addition to holding all the counties that Vice President Kamala Harris won in the 2024 presidential election, Colom won 18 counties President Donald Trump carried that year, including 10 counties Trump won in 2020. Hyde-Smith, who was typical of this year’s incumbent Republicans who seemed clueless about how to campaign in a competitive race, got about 300,000 fewer votes than Trump did two years ago. Colom got thousands more votes than Harris.

Voter turnout typically falls off a cliff between a presidential election and a midterm, but in this race, turnout in Mississippi’s majority-Black counties was 88% of turnout in 2024, while the turnout everywhere else was 75% of 2024’s turnout. According to The New York Times Voter Trends, Colom won more than 90% of the Black vote and, significantly, 25% of the white vote.

During his victory speech, Colom spoke about the faith of voting rights activist Fannie Lou Hamer — who was beaten nearly to death by police in 1963 — and Medgar Evers, the NAACP field secretary who was assassinated outside his Jackson home three days later. 

During his victory speech Wednesday night, Colom spoke broadly about faith, but also about the faith of two Mississippians in particular: voting rights activist Fannie Lou Hamer — who was beaten nearly to death by police in Winona on June 9, 1963 — and Medgar Evers, the NAACP field secretary who was assassinated outside his Jackson home three days later. Colom understood the moment. It would have been impossible for him to have faith that he could win his election without their prerequisite faith that Black Mississippians would someday participate in elections.

In 1964, the year before the Voting Rights Act was signed, the Southern Regional Council’s Voter Education Project reported that Mississippi “presents more resistance to would-be Negro voters than any other state and offers more intimidation and violence to Negroes than all the others combined.” In two years of working to register Black voters, the report said, activists had signed up more people in small cities like Brunswick, Georgia, and Winston-Salem, North Carolina, than in all of Mississippi.

Only an estimated 6.7% of voting-age Black Mississippians were registered in 1964. I asked around this year and wasn’t given the name of anybody in my big Mississippi family who was in that number, not even the ones with college degrees.

Now, 62 years later, Black Mississippians made a Black Mississippian a senator.

This has otherwise been a hard year for my home state. Nolan Wells, a Black teenager, mysteriously died while on a boating trip with white friends, and nobody is facing charges. A white Senatobia police officer fired his gun into a moving car outside Walmart and killed Kohen Wiley, a 1-year-old Black baby. And not only are there no charges, but the state’s attorney general determined the police officer's use of force was justified. The U.S. Supreme Court hollowed out the Voting Rights Act, and some white elected officials in Mississippi, taking cues from their segregationist forefathers, openly discussed wiping out Black voters’ political strength.

On Sept. 22, the day the grand jury declined to bring charges in Wells’ death, I asked on Facebook, “Black people, what’s it like being in Mississippi right now?” The responses included “scary and sad,” “terrible and I want to leave” and “frustrated and disappointed.” A high school classmate used the word “exhausting.”

Some white elected officials in Mississippi, taking cues from their segregationist forefathers, openly discussed wiping out Black voters’ political strength.

We can’t say, then, that Mississippi is transformed. King’s utopian dream notwithstanding, the state transforming may be as good as it gets.

But we can still rejoice in the incompleteness. Between Election Day and Colom being declared the winner, my exhausted classmate acknowledged “the first glimmer of hope and optimism I’ve felt in a long time.”

This is not the first time Black Mississippians have cheered an election, not when 98% chose Barack Obama in 2008 and 96% did in 2012. And not when 94% supported the 2020 ticket that made Kamala Harris the first Black woman vice president. But those historic victories can be credited to the rest of country. Mississippi didn’t go to either of those candidates.

Wednesday night was different. Black Mississippians were joyous because they saw their prayers and their labor pay off — even in Mississippi.
news.author: Symone D. Sanders Townsend

news.title: No One Knows What Really Just Happened in Michigan
news.text:
Abdul El-Sayed arrived to the Capitol on Monday as a senator-elect with the air of a rising political force. Since his win last week over Mike Rogers in Michigan, he’s been on a ubiquitous media tour, confronting issues like U.S. support for Israel and healthcare for all (he offered to name the bill “Trumpcare” if they got it done) with the same brashness he had during the campaign. He posed for beaming photos with other newly elected Democrats and posted a sly, widely shared shot outside his office with his new name plate. It was clear he was enjoying himself.

It was all hard to reconcile with what I’d seen on the campaign trail barely even a week earlier in Michigan. Polls showed he held an advantage, but it often wasn’t obvious to me from the ground that he could win.

On Election Day, outside Burns Seventh-day Adventist Church in Detroit, a light conversation I had with three men near the entrance took an awkward turn. One had noticed a number of Arab voters, and he wasn’t happy about it. They were “trying to get their guy in there,” he said. Arab-owned corner stores and gas stations, he complained, sold alcohol, tobacco, and vapes that were poisoning the neighborhood. In the best case, an El-Sayed victory would win those business owners favors, the man thought. In the worst, some Arabs would be walking around with bombs strapped to their chests.

Then he looked me in eye and asked, “You’re not one of them, are you?” I told him I was. He didn’t take it back. “Well, that’s what they do in their country,” he said.

Those claims weren’t much worse than the ads I’d seen about El-Sayed on every television I came across. Republican advertisers spent $46 million on attacks invoking Shariah law, dual loyalties to foreign and domestic Muslim groups, terrorism, or 9/11. One ad used a woman in a niqab as a warning about what El-Sayed would bring to Michigan. Two days before the election, Haley Stevens, the Democrat he beat in the primary, accused him of supporting bigotry and endorsed Rogers. I couldn’t claim to be surprised by any of this, exactly—I was a teenager in the immediate post-9/11 years and knew how ugly it could get—but it was still stunning to see.

I first interviewed El-Sayed at his home last April, where he poured me an espresso shot using equipment that looked like it belonged in a laboratory. He reminded me of an older cousin. His Egyptianness was contagious. At one point, I sneezed. “Alhamdulillah,” I said. “Yarhamuk Allah,” he answered without missing a beat. It was the most ordinary exchange between two Muslims, but a remarkable one to have with someone running for the United States Senate.

Even then El-Sayed was confident, but he turned shaky when he reflected on his failed bid for Michigan governor in 2018. “It took me years to heal from that, because I felt like I let everyone down,” he told me then. “I don’t want to stumble. I don’t want to fall. I don’t want to dash anybody’s hopes.”

That helped explain how forcefully El-Sayed went after his critics, and why his swagger—which, to me, seemed a bit exaggerated at times, given how comes off in private—was so important to his new political persona and his supporters. Since Trump took power, Democrats I interviewed over the years talked about the need for a fighter, and a populist who could deliver on policies that polled well.

I understood it on that level. It all felt personal to me, too. How could it not? When people were attacking our ethnicity and religion? I loved watching him punch back, but I also caught myself worrying about how his anger would be perceived. I knew how easily a Muslim man defending himself could be made to look like the dangerous fanatic his opponents wanted people to see. I hated that I was even making that calculation.

Maybe that was part of what I saw changing in front me. In New York, Zohran Mamdani had won without apologizing for being Muslim or abandoning his convictions on Palestine. In Michigan, El-Sayed won with the help of organizers who had spent years trying to make Democrats listen. Muslim Americans gave up on waiting for the country to become more accepting. Instead, they organized, challenged their own party, and made themselves harder to dismiss. After a decade of reporting on the limits placed on Muslim political power, I wondered whether I’d become too used to those limits myself. In Washington now, El-Sayed is about to test that and show what really just happened in Michigan. Even his supporters have some questions.

On election night at the venue where El-Sayed supporters gathered, confident and nervous at once, people ate sliders (beef, not pork) and macaroni and cheese and watched results come in from everywhere but Michigan. Then at about 1:30 a.m. on Wednesday, El-Sayed stepped onto the stage in downtown Detroit and said his whole name into the microphone.

“My name is Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed, and I am so proud and honored to stand here as your senator-elect.”

The room nearly tore itself apart. I thought I had a pretty good view of the stage until everyone’s phones shot up. Somewhere behind me, an older woman let out a zaghrouta, the ululation you hear at Arab weddings.

“Up until right about now, you might have noticed I always say ‘inshallah,’ or ‘God willing,’ whenever the outcome of this race was mentioned.” He continued, “But today, tonight, we can turn that inshallah into a—”

“Alhamdulillah!” the room shouted. “For the right-wing ops, that just means ‘Praise be to God,’ ” he added.

I texted my editor. Had the race been called somewhere and I missed it? It hadn’t. But he declared victory anyway. (El-Sayed later said Rogers never bothered to call him to concede.)

Everywhere I looked, I recognized another face from years of reporting on Muslims and politics, except I was used to seeing these people angry, exhausted, or pleading with someone in power to listen. Now they were cheering, shouting over one another, holding phones above their heads to capture a moment they had spent years working toward—Linda Sarsour, Mahmoud Khalil, Wajahat Ali, Kashif Shaikh, Amani Al-Khatahtbeh, Rima Mohammad, Rania Batrice, Mehdi Hasan, Prem Thakker livestreaming from a corner. Many had come from New York, California, Washington, Texas, or elsewhere. (Notably not in attendance: Hasan Piker, a name I’m pretty sure El-Sayed would rather never hear again.)

I knew many of these people from a decade of reporting on the often ugly intersection of Muslims and American politics. One of them, Khalil, is still fighting the government’s effort to deport him over his activism. Now here they were, celebrating the first Muslim elected to the Senate. It felt like 10 years of exclusion from politics had culminated into a single moment in that room.

But even amid all that celebrating, many were looking ahead—and they weren’t entirely sure what they saw. Qasim Rashid, a prominent human rights lawyer and activist, was sanguine but cautious. “We love Abdul, but we need to hold him accountable now,” he told me. He wasn’t alone.

In 2016, when it still seemed unlikely Donald Trump would become president, I’d gone to the Republican National Convention in Cleveland to take pictures, and a man dressed as Thomas Jefferson approached me, asked if I was Muslim, and, when I said yes, told me Islam was evil.

Meanwhile, Muslim Americans like Rashida Tlaib and Ilhan Omar became the first Muslim women in Congress in 2018. Organizers registered voters, built coalitions and institutions, and tried to move politics beyond the question of whether they belonged here at all. I watched Muslim American life become louder and more assured, as actors like Ramy Youssef and Mo Amer modeled success in entertainment. There were disagreements within our community, too, about how much to compromise. And then Gaza made that argument impossible.

I began spending real time in Dearborn, Michigan, in spring 2024, when Arab and Muslim voters told me they were willing to hand Trump back the presidency to punish Democrats over Gaza. “Uncommitted” movement organizers Layla Elabed and Abbas Alawieh warned Democrats that their Israel policy could cost them the election. At the Democratic National Convention that summer, I followed the movement’s 30 delegates, representing some 700,000 voters, as they tried to persuade party leaders to let a Palestinian American doctor who’d worked in Gaza speak. After days of evasions, the answer was no. I watched Alawieh sit outside the United Center, head in his hands, refusing to leave.

He voted for Kamala Harris anyway, but Trump won Michigan and returned to office. Trump’s administration turbocharged immigration enforcement and targeted pro-Palestinian activists. The Democratic National Committee later left Gaza out of its postelection autopsy.

The next time I saw Alawieh, he was at a convention in Michigan, campaigning in the same halls as El-Sayed while running for state Senate himself. On Tuesday night, a few hours before El-Sayed declared victory, a newly elected Alawieh stood before his family in Dearborn’s Byblos Banquet Center and declared, “We’re making history.” He explained the lesson of Uncommitted plainly: “We have to become the leaders ourselves.” And he had a warning. “The path to the presidency in 2028,” he said, “will come through our communities here in southeastern Michigan, and we will have questions.”

His father also spoke. “If you want to invest, brothers, invest in your children before you invest in smoke shops and gas stations,” he said in Arabic. He was serious, but I laughed—It sounded a little too close to an Arab dad humblebragging. Then he addressed the president directly. “We want to break this taboo that Arab Americans can’t be the first. It’s not one Abdul coming for you, Trump. Thousands of Abduls are coming for you.”

El-Sayed wasn’t exactly created by Uncommitted. He made healthcare, affordability, and getting money out of politics central to his politics from the beginning. He supported the Uncommitted protest vote in 2024, then endorsed Harris. He never promised disillusioned Muslim voters a party that would agree with them on everything. But he is giving them a reason to believe they could change it. Now, in a new moment of new Muslim political power, they’re watching—closely. If El-Sayed is going to be a new face of the Democrats, they expect him to turn into the senator he promised them he’d be.

Back onstage in Detroit, El-Sayed had a message for the parents who’d spent the campaign explaining to their children why the president was mocking a Muslim man’s name and faith: “Let them know tomorrow that the bad guys lost.” To Rogers, he declared, “You chose hate, and Michigan chose hope.” And Trump, who had spent months trying to make El-Sayed’s name sound threatening, could now just call him “Senator.”

It was an extraordinary night for Democrats everywhere. They were projected to retake both chambers. Texas, of all places, had elected a Democratic senator and governor for the first time in three decades, including its first Latina governor, Gina Hinojosa. Latino voters, who had swung toward Trump in 2024, came roaring back toward Democrats. Roughly 7 in 10 Hispanic voters in Texas backed James Talarico for Senate. El-Sayed was hardly the only historic first: Georgia elected the country’s first Black woman governor, New Mexico the first Native American woman governor, Minnesota the first Native American woman senator, and New Hampshire the first openly gay male senator.

There were plenty of explanations for this blue wave that had nothing to do with Muslims or Palestine: anger over prices that still hadn’t come down, belligerent ICE raids and deportations, a new war in Iran, a cover-up of the Epstein files, and a broader backlash against an administration that had alienated voters who’d supported it just two years earlier.

Exit polls suggested that economic frustration and opposition to Trump gave Democrats the edge. So what could El-Sayed’s victory really tell us about the power of Islamophobia? Had Americans become more willing to elect a Muslim because of his faith, or were they so fed up with Republicans that even an extraordinarily ugly campaign couldn’t change their minds?

I’d spent Tuesday driving between polling places in Michigan, and what I heard gave me reasons to doubt a simple answer.

There was the exchange I had in Detroit. Then, in West Bloomfield, outside Congregation B’nai Moshe, a synagogue, Gordon Geist, a Republican, was handing out literature for a group called Democrats for Mike Rogers. He told me he was a devout Christian and a patriotic American: “I struggle with Islam, with the rabid aspects of Islam, the radical aspects of Islam.” He claimed El-Sayed was supported by the Muslim Brotherhood, a repeated falsehood in right-wing circles.

Then he invoked taqiyya, a religious concept of self-preservation that anti-Muslim activists distort into the claim that Muslims lie to non-Muslims and have a secret plan to take over. He took it as reason to doubt anything El-Sayed said, including about healthcare. “How can you trust a word he says?” he asked me. Rogers, on the other hand, was “a patriot,” he said. “He’s a proven guy. He loves America.”

I thought of the less dramatic work I’d watched Mamdani do in New York before his victory: a political speech in a mosque basement, followed by an announcement about somebody’s badly parked car; volunteers passing out flyers as he moved through Chaand Raat celebrations in the Bronx and Queens. None of it looked like history at the time.

That groundwork is necessary to withstand enormous spending. Like in Mamdani’s race, the American Israel Public Affairs Committee and affiliated groups spent close to $30 million backing El-Sayed’s opponent in the primary, and an AIPAC-linked super PAC reportedly spent another $12.7 million attacking him in the general election. This was not a contest between Jews and Muslims—exit polls suggested that a majority of Jewish voters backed El-Sayed. But the results did call into question the idea that powerful pro-Israel groups could make a candidate’s position on Palestine disqualifying, no matter how much they spent.

None of this proves that a Muslim candidate can now win anywhere, or that the attacks somehow helped El-Sayed. Michigan is not every state. Mamdani and El-Sayed both ran on affordability, not shattering the glass ceiling for Muslims. And though in both races I personally met people who still saw Islam as a reason to think a candidate is dangerous, what the results showed was that those suspicions hadn’t been enough.

In Dearborn that day, I’d watched groups of women in niqabs walk into McDonald Elementary to vote. For weeks, a Republican ad had used the image of a woman dressed like them as a warning about the future of Michigan should El-Sayed win. There was something delightful about watching those women be represented as something frightening in the evening, then seeing them show up to the polls the next morning. The man at the church in Detroit might never change his mind about people like them, or about people like me. Maybe the change wasn’t that he suddenly had to. Maybe it was that we no longer needed him to in order to win.

El-Sayed’s first week in Washington was thrilling, but also an anxious one, even for some of his own supporters. He has probably just signed up for six years as a Fox News villain, bringing in a new round of conspiracies and backlash. And then there’s the question of the kind of senator he will turn out to be. But for the first time, late on election night, I let myself dream a little. I wondered whether my kids might grow up without that familiar feeling of having to prove they belong here. Maybe one day I’ll try to explain it to them, and they won’t have any idea what I’m talking about.
news.summary: Abdul El-Sayed’s election result was seismic—but even his supporters aren’t sure what it means.
news.author: Aymann Ismail

news.title: Vance, Rubio, Jon Ossoff & Pete Buttigieg lead 2028 White House race in post-midterm survey
news.text:
Following the midterms' Blue Wave, White House hopefuls have begun testing the waters for their campaigns — and four top contenders have emerged for the 2028 presidential contest.
According to a Reuters/Ipsos survey, Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio are the frontrunners for the Republican nomination, while Georgia Senator Jon Ossoff and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg have emerged as the favourites among Democrats.
Among Republicans, 45 per cent of voters said Rubio would be an excellent presidential candidate, and 43 per cent said the same for Vance.
Ossoff emerges as Democrats' rising star
With his re-election in Georgia, Ossoff has emerged as the most popular face among Democrats.
While Ossoff and Buttigieg were both the top choices of 29 per cent of Democrats, Ossoff was much more recognisable.
While about one in five Democrats said they had never heard of Buttigieg, one in three said they had never heard of Ossoff.
ALSO READ: Centrist or woke? After Blue Wave, Democrats debate their future — and that matters for 2028
Coming off his victorious midterm campaign, Ossoff has momentum as well as recognition on his side. He has made headlines by calling President Donald Trump corrupt and unfit for office in unusually direct language that has resonated with voters. He won re-election by 18 percentage points in a state that Trump had wo in the 2024 election.
Observers have often compared Ossoff's speech and debating style to that of former President Barack Obama, who remains the most popular living Democrat.
But there are also other well-known Democrats in the fray, such as former Vice President Kamala Harris and outgoing California Governor Gavin Newsom.
The survey found that Democrats saw both Newsom and Harris, who lost the 2024 election to Trump, as excellent candidates with 23 per cent support. They polled higher than progressive Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, who was backed by 15 per cent of Democrats.
Vance no longer Trump's heir apparent
While Vance was considered Trump's natural successor in 2028, his ambitions have taken a hit in recent months. Not only has Trump refused to endorse him, or anyone else for that matter, but Vance's prospects have also been affected by the president's deep unpopularity.
Additionally, there are signs that a rift could be developing between Trump and Vance after the midterms. Vance broke ranks with Trump to say that the war with Iran was the main reason for the historic defeat. Days later, Trump took Vance off the team holding negotiations with Iran and tasked him with checking purported crime and corruption in states run by the Democratic Party.
There are around a dozen other Republicans understood to have presidential ambitions, with outgoing Florida Governor Ron DeSantis having the best rating of 32 per cent among Republicans. Others, such as Trump's son Donald Trump Jr and Texas Senator Ted Cruz, remain polarising figures.

news.title: Next Time, Impeach Pete Hegseth for Press Censorship
news.text:
Before the effort to impeach him failed Tuesday, Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth lashed out at a group he despises even more than “beardos” and “weirdos”: the press. His security team threatened to physically remove journalists from a news briefing, Hegseth’s first in several months, if they didn’t maintain decorum. 

It’s nothing new for Hegseth. He may want to pump soldiers up with testosterone, but he’s spent the last couple years trying to neuter the Fourth Estate. It’s unfortunate that his unconstitutional attacks on journalists were not part of the official case for removing him. Next time, they should be. And Congress should not stop with Hegseth. 

The impeachment resolution Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., brought against Hegseth included eight articles, alleging that the so-called Secretary of War acted illegally in military campaigns in Iran, Venezuela, and the Caribbean, among other things. The resolution touched on free speech violations – Article VI is about Hegseth’s retaliation campaign against Sen. Mark Kelly, D-Ariz., for reminding troops of their right to refuse illegal orders – but it didn’t mention the press. 

A recap is in order: In February of 2025, Hegseth’s Pentagon evicted the New York Times, NBC, Politico, and NPR from their dedicated workspaces in the building, replacing them largely with sycophantic right-wing outlets like Breitbart and One America News Network. Some elements of the fawning right-wing press were on full display during his Tuesday press conference: “How does it make you feel,” asked a reporter from an outlet called Real America’s Voice, “when our own politicians don’t support taking out the narco-traffickers that kill their own constituents?” 

Months later, Hegseth concocted a requirement that journalists who wish to access the Pentagon pledge not to solicit unauthorized information from the government, under threat of losing their credentials. Dozens of reporters from outlets across the political spectrum turned in their access badges rather than comply. They were replaced, once again, by loyalists who could be counted on to treat Hegseth and his fragile ego with kid gloves. 

A judge soon struck down the pledge policy as an unconstitutional effort to force out disfavored journalists. The Pentagon immediately issued new restrictions on unauthorized disclosures that were, in some ways, even worse than the originals. The judge rejected that policy too. Hegseth also imposed a requirement for reporters to be escorted around the Pentagon, which is still working its way through the courts. 

Hegseth’s Pentagon cracked down on the military’s newspaper, Stars and Stripes, barring it from briefings and demanding it stop publishing “woke” content. After all, it used to run columns from that well-known leftist Ann Coulter. His Pentagon then fired key personnel and otherwise did everything it could think of to try to turn Stars and Stripes into a propaganda organ unrecognizable to its readership – mostly troops, veterans, and their families. 

It gets even pettier: Hegseth’s staff barred press photographers from briefings after they published pictures of him that he found unflattering.

Hegseth’s illegal war on transparency has extended not just to reporters but also to their sources. He forced staff to take unreliable polygraph tests to identify leakers until the White House itself halted the effort after a Trump loyalist complained about being targeted. He’s formed a joint task force with the Justice Department to push for prosecution of leakers and adopted President Donald Trump’s alarming habit of equating national security reporting to “treason.” 

There will almost certainly be another effort to impeach Hegseth in the next Congress, if not sooner. Censorship may not be the lede — alleged international war crimes understandably tend to take the spotlight over other infractions — but it also shouldn’t be an afterthought. 

While Congress is at it, remove Brendan Carr too

And while they’re impeaching wartime censors, Congress shouldn’t forget about FCC Chair Brendan Carr. He has defied federal law, the First Amendment, and the FCC’s own rules and guidelines in his incessant efforts to turn the agency into Trump’s journalism police. And critical reporting on the Iran war – which the Republican party now apparently agrees deserved criticism all along – has been one of Carr’s most frequent targets. 

At the beginning of the war, after Trump fumed at accurate coverage he disliked, Carr – who wears Trump’s gilded face as a lapel pin and sips from a mug depicting himself as Trump’s pit bull – promptly reposted the president’s attack. He warned that broadcasters airing “hoaxes and news distortions” should “correct course before their license renewals come up.” 

An emboldened Trump responded the same night, posting that outlets spreading “fake news” about the war should “be brought up on Charges for TREASON,” adding that he was “thrilled” Carr was investigating the licenses of media outlets across the country.

Then, after April’s purported ceasefire, CNN reported a statement from Iran’s Supreme National Security Council claiming victory. Trump took to Truth Social to announce a purported investigation into whether CNN committed some unspecified crime by publishing the quote. Carr piled on, accusing CNN, which the FCC does not regulate, of pushing a “hoax headline” that “requires accountability,” implying that licensees who aired similar reporting would face his wrath. But the statement was real. Trump just would’ve preferred CNN air a different one. 

Of course, Carr’s censorship campaigns are myriad and many have little to do with the war. But his arguably most egregious (and impeachable) offense did, albeit indirectly. 

Last year, Carr inexplicably stalled the FCC’s consideration of then-CBS News parent Paramount’s merger with David Ellison’s Skydance until Paramount paid $16 million to settle Trump’s frivolous lawsuit over “60 Minutes’” editing of an interview with Kamala Harris. He approved the merger two days after Trump said he’d received his dirty money. Essentially, he aided Trump in laundering a bribe through the courts.

Carr – who knows better, having once written that editorial judgment “should be beyond the reach of any government official” – also used his leverage over the merger to give himself and his delegates a seat at CBS’s editors desk, extracting unconstitutional editorial concessions from Ellison’s team. CBS has since been widely criticized for softening its coverage of Trump’s agenda, including (among other things) echoing administration narratives on the U.S. military operations like the war in Iran and the abduction of Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro.

Facilitating likely bribery is the epitome of an impeachable offense. Republicans might not vote for impeachment, but after all the backlash Carr has received from the right, they also can’t credibly accuse Democrats of some kind of partisan witch hunt. Congress should not let the opportunity to hold Carr accountable pass them by.

Lawmakers need to acknowledge that the reporters the administration called traitors got it right all along, and that those who attempted to censor wartime journalism did a disservice to the Constitution and the American people. Hegseth and Carr should both be impeached, with the press they tried to muzzle freely reporting on every minute of the proceedings.
news.author: Seth Stern

news.title: These two voter turnout trends explain what happened across the South in the election
news.text:
Democratic victories in the South this year were driven just as much by who showed up to vote as who stayed home, according to an NPR analysis of turnout data.

Midterm elections normally have lower voter participation than presidential contests. But from Louisiana to the Carolinas, counties that voted for former Vice President Kamala Harris in 2024 came closer to matching — and in some cases exceeding — presidential turnout. At the same time, counties won by President Trump saw a much sharper decline in turnout and fewer Republican votes.

In six southern states — Louisiana, Mississippi, Alabama, Georgia, South Carolina and North Carolina — turnout dropped by 19% in Harris-won counties compared to 26% in Trump-won counties. (In Louisiana, counties are called parishes).

Across the South, the six states analyzed swung an average of 22 points towards Democrats, larger than the national swing of about 14.5 points.

This differential turnout was a key factor in Democrats flipping Senate seats in North Carolina, South Carolina and Mississippi, and contributed to the closer-than-expected margin in Louisiana's Senate race.

In Mississippi, Democrat Scott Colom outperformed Harris, earning roughly 8,100 more votes than she did in 2024. Colom's margin over incumbent Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith is just over 5,600 votes as final ballots are being tallied.

Democratic Senate nominees in those six states earned more raw votes than Harris in 170 counties. On the flip side, the Republican nominees garnered hundreds of thousands fewer votes than Trump.

Black voters showed up

In special elections and primaries leading up to the midterms, voting data and polls showed a surge in Black voter participation, spurred in part by a Supreme Court decision that gutted part of the Voting Rights Act.

The Louisiana v. Callais decision led to changed congressional maps across the South, including Tennessee, Alabama, Louisiana and North Carolina. After redrawing boundary lines in a way that aimed to elect an 11-3 Republican majority delegation, North Carolina Democrats are now on track to hold an 11-3 majority.

Majority-Black counties overall had a higher voter turnout with about 85% compared to 76% for white, non-Hispanic majority counties. Sixteen majority-Black counties had more Democratic votes than during the 2024 election, with 12 of them in Mississippi. Clay County, Miss., had the largest voter turnout increase — by 17 points from 2024 to 2026.

Beyond majority-Black turnout, Democratic candidates in these southern states benefitted from a smaller drop in turnout from the 2024 election.

In Georgia, Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff finished with roughly 79,000 fewer votes than former Vice President Kamala Harris won in the state two years prior, despite there being more than a million fewer total votes overall. 

All 159 counties in Georgia shifted towards Democrats. Ossoff flipped a dozen of them, including suburban Fayette County, on the way to a 14 point victory.

South Carolina had some of the largest Democratic voter turnout, with Greenville, Spartanburg, and Lexington counties having the largest increases in raw Democratic votes from the 2024 election. Greenville, which backed Trump by 20 points two years ago, flipped to support Sen.-elect Annie Andrews by about two points.

Republicans voters did not

Nowhere was the Republican drop off more stark than in North Carolina, where former Gov. Roy Cooper flipped the Senate race by a 20 point margin. Former Republican National Committee Chair Michael Whatley earned 1.25 million fewer votes than Trump did when he carried the state in 2024, a roughly 43% drop in GOP support. 

No county or parish across these southern states came close to matching Trump 2024 vote totals. The lowest drop off came in Greene County, Ga. with 83%, the only one of 518 counties where Republicans earned more than 80% of Trump's 2024 raw votes.

The largest drop off came in North Carolina, which saw only two-thirds of the Republican votes they did in 2024. Wake and Mecklenburg counties, home to the two largest cities — Raleigh and Charlotte — saw the biggest drops, with about 100,000 and 90,000 fewer GOP voters respectively.

Atlanta and its suburbs also saw a notable decline in support for Republicans, with Fulton, Gwinnett, Cobb, DeKalb and Cherokee counties losing between 35,000 and 77,000 GOP votes each. Democrats saw smaller losses in those areas, with slight gains in votes for Gwinnett and Cherokee counties.
news.summary: In six states across the Deep South, a drastic swing to the left this election was driven by high Black voter turnout and compounded by a sharp decline in voting rates across Republican-heavy areas.
news.author: Stephen Fowler

news.title: ‘They had to nerf the coolest movie star’: Arnold Schwarzenegger’s Republican stance prompts criticism
news.text: Veteran actor and former governor of California, Arnold Schwarzenegger, went viral on social media following his appearance at Jimmy Kimmel Live.The fame stood by his affiliation with the Republican Party, even as the host questioned the party’s conservative direction, in light of the GOP’s changing political history. His statement sparked backlash from social media users. So, how did the criticism emerge? Here's what we know of the incident. The controversy emerged after the former California governor appeared on Jimmy Kimmel Live, on Wednesday, November 11. In correspondence with Kimmel, the 79-year-old actor stood by his Republican identity. When asked what being a Republican means, he claimed, “A traditional republican is someone that admires the republican for having freeing the slaves.”Kimmel quipped that the GOP no longer takes credit for that. However, Schwarzenegger maintained, “This is the history. This is what I’m about.”Despite being reminded that these values are no longer associated with the party, the star maintained that he defined his identity around a historical view of the party. He explained that his brand of politics follows figures like Ronald Reagan, who created the California Air Resources Board in 1967, and Richard Nixon, who created the EPA. They represented Republicans who crossed the aisle to work with Democrats, “to get things done”. Following his Republican stance, the star criticized single-party unilateral approaches as ineffective. He stated that in order to ensure development, Republicans and Democrats must work together. “This is the only way you can accomplish something rather than always pointing fingers and accusing each other of things and calling each other names… You have to get together and accomplish and be a public servant rather than a party servant. There’s a difference.”The actor's statement sparked criticism from several social media users who condemned Schwarzenegger for holding on to a historic view of the party. An X user wrote, “Does he realize that the progressive republicans that freed the slaves quite literally do not exist anymore or what”, while another shared, “They had to nerf the coolest movie star ever somehow I guess.”More reactions: However, others weighed in to defend the veteran actor, citing his endorsement of Kamala Harris. Despite his Republican affiliation, Arnold Schwarzenegger had previously endorsed Democrat Kamala Harris ahead of the 2024 elections, over Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance. His political stance has emerged as a subject of significant discourse.
news.author: Anwesha Saha

news.title: Newsom reveals when he'll decide on 2028 White House bid amid growing speculation
news.text: Democratic California Gov. Gavin Newsom said Thursday that he will decide within the next two months whether to seek the presidency, revealing that he plans to make up his mind by early January about a potential 2028 bid. Newsom, who will leave office in January, was asked about his presidential aspirations while attending the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference in Antalya, Turkey. "As it relates to 2028, we'll make that decision in the next few months," Newsom told Turkey's Anadolu news agency. "I'll make the determination at the beginning of the year," he continued. "So we'll spend the next few weeks with the family and make a decision early January." GAVIN NEWSOM SEEKS COUNSEL FROM ‘MASTER’ BILL CLINTON AS HE PLOTS PROJECT 2029 Newsom has long been discussed as a potential 2028 contender, frequently mentioned among possible Democratic candidates, including Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., and Sen. Jon Ossoff, D-Ga. However, fellow Californian and 2024 Democratic presidential nominee Kamala Harris could complicate Newsom's plans if she decides to launch another White House bid. news.title: Newsom reveals when he'll decide on 2028 White House bid amid growing speculation
news.text:
Democratic California Gov. Gavin Newsom said Thursday that he will decide within the next two months whether to seek the presidency, revealing that he plans to make up his mind by early January about a potential 2028 bid.

Newsom, who will leave office in January, was asked about his presidential aspirations while attending the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference in Antalya, Turkey.

"As it relates to 2028, we'll make that decision in the next few months," Newsom told Turkey's Anadolu news agency.

"I'll make the determination at the beginning of the year," he continued. "So we'll spend the next few weeks with the family and make a decision early January."

Newsom has long been discussed as a potential 2028 contender, frequently mentioned among possible Democratic candidates, including Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., and Sen. Jon Ossoff, D-Ga.

However, fellow Californian and 2024 Democratic presidential nominee Kamala Harris could complicate Newsom's plans if she decides to launch another White House bid.

Newsom previously said he would not run for president if Harris entered the race.

"I don't know if she runs, but we'll see," Newsom told CNN's Jake Tapper in a September interview. "But I wouldn't run if she ran."

"If she runs, you will not," Tapper responded.

"Of course not. Why would I?" Newsom said. "I wouldn't do that to her ... I wouldn't do that to you. I wouldn't waste everyone's time. Who needs that?"

Newsom also suggested during the interview that spectators would feast on the "mutual-assured destruction" among Democrats competing for the nomination.

"I mean, you do whatever you want. I don't care," Tapper told Newsom. "But [the] counterargument would be, like, you know, she had her shot. And you've never run, and she's run twice."

"Yeah," Newsom responded. "I mean, that'd be the approach to the campaign, certainly. That'd be the case you'd make. Pretty good one, actually. That's objectively true."

Newsom, who is term-limited after 2026, outlined his political timeline just over a week after Republicans suffered sweeping defeats in the midterm elections, losing control of both chambers of Congress and several traditionally Republican strongholds.

Newsom said he was "particularly pleased with the outcome of the election."

"Donald Trump's presidency, as we know it, ended last week in the U.S.," he said. "It was an historic rebuke of his tenure and now it's incumbent upon those that were successful to govern and to lead my party. The Democratic Party now has to set forth a positive alternative agenda to Donald Trump."

Fox News Digital's Joseph A. Wulfsohn contributed to this report.

news.title: 2028 White House Race: 4 Potential Contenders Catching Voters' Attention
news.text: Four potential contenders in the 2028 race for the White House have caught American voters' attention with their early jockeying: Republicans JD Vance and Marco Rubio and Democrats Jon Ossoff and Pete Buttigieg, according to the latest Reuters/Ipsos poll.None of the four has yet formally launched a campaign and the parties' 2028 nominating contests are more than a year away, leaving plenty of time for new contenders to emerge and for voters' views to change.Some 45% of Republican voters polled said they believed Secretary of State Rubio would be an "excellent" presidential candidate, with 43% saying the same of Vice President Vance. Former Transportation Secretary Buttigieg and US Senator Ossoff, of Georgia, each got that rating from 29% of Democratic voters.The poll, which surveyed 1,705 US adults nationwide including roughly 500 registered voters from each party and was completed on Monday, had a margin of error of 5 percentage points for Republican and Democratic voters.President Donald Trump, struggling with an approval rating near the lowest of his career, looms large over the conversation for both parties. Republicans are divided on whether they want a candidate who breaks with Trump or follows in his footsteps, while Democrats, who are flying high after routing Republicans in the November 3 congressional elections, are divided on how aggressively to go after the president, such as through impeachment.Trump has quizzed allies on whom they prefer Vance or Rubio and in a Sunday interview with CBS's "60 Minutes" said he would "not necessarily" make an endorsement in the Republican primary.'MANAGED TO DO HIS JOB'Barbara Rezner, an attorney in Florida who voted for Trump in the last three presidential elections, said she prefers Rubio over Vance, whom she considers too far to the right and too close to the president."Rubio has managed to do his job. He's stayed off most people's radar because he hasn't done anything too far left, too far right, too crazy," Rezner said.The modest but growing dissatisfaction with Trump among Republicans is centered on the president's decision to launch a war on Iran that has driven fuel prices higher. Rubio has been notably absent from many of the so-far fruitless peace talks with Iran despite being the nation's top diplomat. Vance has shown signs of wanting to distance himself as well, saying publicly that the Republican drubbing in the midterm elections owed to the war with Iran.A dozen-odd other Republicans are also in the national conversation over 2028 contenders, with Florida Governor Ron DeSantis among the best regarded, with 32% of Republicans rating him as an excellent option. Others - like Trump's son, Donald Trump Jr., and Texas US Senator Ted Cruz - have their fans, but also many detractors.OSSOFF AND BUTTIGIEGAmong Democrats, Ossoff is at the top of many voters' lists, with 29% of the party's registered voters rating him as excellent. Ossoff has grabbed headlines in recent months by calling Trump corrupt and unfit for office in unusually direct language, and last week he won his re-election race by 18 percentage points in Georgia, a state Trump carried by 2 points in 2024.Buttigieg also gets the excellent rating from 29% of Democrats. Buttigieg also ran for president in 2020 and is better known nationally than Ossoff.About one in five Democrats say they have never heard of Buttigieg, compared to roughly one in three who say the same about Ossoff. Very few Republicans are unfamiliar with Vance, but about one in six said they do not know who Rubio is. For candidates in either party, starting the election cycle with more name recognition can save money that would be spent getting the candidate's name out, but examples abound of little-known candidates catching fire during the campaign, as happened with former President Bill Clinton.Buttigieg and Ossoff are considered moderates among Democrats, and that appeals to Democratic voters like Ed Blair, a retired pig farmer in southern Illinois, who gives Buttigieg a better rating in part because Ossoff is less familiar."I do favor the more moderate candidates over the more progressive ones," said Blair, who is wary of proposed major shifts like expanding federal Medicare health insurance coverage from all seniors to everyone in the country. Blair would prefer gradual shifts, such as expanding Medicare to cover all children. "In going towards some of the progressive policies, small steps need to be taken rather than large ones to give people time to adapt."The Reuters/Ipsos poll shows other well-known moderates - like former Vice President Kamala Harris, who lost to Trump in the 2024 presidential election, and California Governor Gavin Newsom - each get "excellent candidate" ratings of 23%, higher than the 15% of Democrats who view progressive stalwart Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, a US representative for New York, that way.Ocasio-Cortez told CNN after the midterms that impeaching Trump should be an option on the table, while Buttigieg told the New Yorker magazine he is "not very interested" in impeachment.Elaine Kamarck, a Democratic strategist, cautioned against reading too deeply into the public's current views this far out from the 2028 election. "It's a world away," Kamarck said. "There are lots of people in both parties who are still deciding if they are going to run. You might be able to predict who will run, but you certainly don't know anything about who is going to be ahead."(Except for the headline, this story has not been edited by NDTV staff and is published from a syndicated feed.)

news.title: Trump Says He'd Beat Obama 'Easily' in Potential Presidential Race
news.text: President Donald Trump said that he could "easily" beat former President Barack Obama in a hypothetical matchup, while calling his predecessor "highly overrated." In a sit-down with Stephen A. Smith on Smith's podcast Straight Shooter on Thursday, Trump said, "I got many more votes than he got. And I got many more votes in the states...I have most of the state records of the big states. If you take a look at Texas, I have the all-time record, Florida I have the all-time record." Smith then asked Trump if he was implying that he'd beat Obama, "Yeah, I think I'd beat him easily, yeah. I think he's highly overrated." In the 2024 presidential election, Trump won all the swing states and the popular vote with 77,304,290 votes compared to Vice President Kamala Harris' 75,019,761 votes. In the 2012 election, Obama defeated Republican Mitt Romney with 62,611,250 votes compared to 59,134,475 votes. Trump's remarks to Smith come on the heels of sweeping midterm losses for the Republican Party that saw House and Senate majority flip in favor of the Democrats. The president conceded partially that the landslide Democratic wins could be due to the war in Iran, although he said he would still do it again. Similarly, Democrats lost the midterms in 2010 while Obama was in office. Newsweek reached out to the office of Barack and Michelle Obama via online portal Thursday night for comment. What To Know In his comments to Smith about Obama, Trump added, "I just think, that's just my opinion, I think he's overrated. I didn't think he was a good president, I thought he was a divider." Smith then asked Trump how he'd classify himself, which he answered, "as a person that brings people together." In the 2024 presidential election cycle, Trump obtained 6,110,125 votes in Florida versus 4,683,038 votes for Harris, according to the Florida Department of State Division of Elections. In 2012, Obama obtained 4,237,756 votes in the Sunshine State and Romney landed 4,163,447 votes. In state voting data reviewed by Newsweek dating over 40 years, Trump had the most votes for a presidential nominee in Florida. In Texas, Trump obtained 6,393,597 votes compared to Harris' 4,835,250 votes in the 2024 presidential election. In 2012, Obama had 3,294,440 votes in the Lone Star State compared to Romney's 4,555,799 votes. Newsweek also reviewed state voting data going back decades in Texas, and Trump had the most votes out of any presidential nominee. Texas has been known as a Republican stronghold for presidential elections, and Florida has shifted to the right over time and is now also seen as a reliable pickup for GOP presidential candidates. Robert Collins, professor of public policy at Dillard University, told Newsweek on Thursday: "This is clearly just President Trump throwing red meat to his base. Given the president currently has a national job approval rating in the 30s, no rational observer believes he could beat Obama in a head-to-head matchup right now. "His past remarks on the possibility of running for a third term are also just trying to keep his base happy. No serious constitutional scholar believes there is any legal way for President Trump to run for a third term." The president's interview with Smith also touched on Iran, working with Democrats during the remainder of his term, gasoline prices, immigration policy and his legacy. Trump and Obama's Popularity & Approval Compared In a CNN-SSRS poll conducted earlier this year, 57 percent said they had a favorable opinion of Obama versus 32 percent who had an unfavorable opinion. Comparatively, Trump had a 34 percent favorability rating versus a 55 percent unfavorable rating. When asked which president they admire the most, Obama landed 30 percent and Trump had 19 percent, the poll shows. The poll was conducted from May 7 to May 31 among 2,480 respondents and had a margin of error of 2.7 percent. In a YouGov/Economist poll this week, Trump's approval rating is 32 percent versus a 63 percent disapproval rating. The poll surveyed 1,685 U.S. citizens from November 9 to November 11 and had a margin of error of 3 percent. In a November 2010 poll after the midterm elections, Obama's approval was 42 percent with a 49 percent disapproval rating, also in a YouGov/Economist poll. Newsweek’s reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story. Learn more about Martyn here. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Edward T. Cummins
news.summary: In a sit down with Stephen A. Smith, Trump took repeated swipes at Obama, while saying he could beat him in a hypothetical race.

news.title: Arnold Schwarzenegger reveals if he's still Republican after blue 'tsunami'
news.text:
Arnold Schwarzenegger isn't switching parties even after Democrats' sweeping victory at the midterm elections.

On a Wednesday, Nov. 11 episode of "Jimmy Kimmel Live!" the former California governor, 79, said he remains a Republican despite not always agreeing with elected officials in the political party.

"Yeah, I’m a Republican, absolutely," he told host Jimmy Kimmel. "A traditional Republican is someone that admires the Republican Party for having freed the slaves."

Kimmel, 58, quipped that the GOP "don’t get credit for that anymore," to which Schwarzenegger replied, "This is the history. This is what I’m about. Someone that has given those slaves American citizenship and given them the rights to vote."

The "Terminator" actor explained that he practices the "Ronald Reagan philosophy," referring to how some Republicans have historically fought for causes now associated with Democrats, citing the 40th U.S. president and former California governor's environmental record, including his role in establishing the California Air Resources Board in 1967.

"That was done by Ronald Reagan, a Republican. Nixon created the EPA," he continued. "He created the Environmental Protection Agency to protect our environment, the water and the air."

After Kimmel said that Schwarzenegger's philosophy "sounds like all the opposite things that the Republican party stands for now," the actor said, "Yeah, but it doesn’t mean I have to change my philosophy."

Schwarzenegger said he urges Republicans to work with Democrats to get "things done," as he said he did while serving as governor.

"Unfortunately, I think you're the only one of them left," Kimmel replied.

"No, I don't think I'm the only one left," Schwarzenegger pushed back.

Arnold Schwarzenegger reveals why he didn't endorse Trump

The "Man with the Bag" star also shared details about conversations he had with President Donald Trump ahead of his first White House term.

"When he ran for the first time for the presidency in 2016, we talked to each other several times and because we had a good relationship, we were very good friends. And he asked me if I would go and endorse him and campaign with him," he told Kimmel.

"I said, 'Donald, I'd like to be your friend, I said, but it happens to be to there are certain things that you stand for, that you're talking about... that I don't believe in."

He cited environmental issues as a polarizing topic between them, telling Trump, "You don't believe there is climate change. You don't believe that there's the threat of pollution," adding, "I've worked on that issue for so many years."

Ahead of the 2024 election, Schwarzenegger endorsed Democrat Kamala Harris over Trump and Vice President JD Vance, writing on X, "I will always be an American before I am a Republican. That’s why, this week, I am voting for Kamala Harris and Tim Walz."

Reacting to Democrats' victory in the Nov. 3 midterm elections, which will give the party control of both chambers of Congress, Schwarzenegger described the results as a blue "tsunami" and said the political landscape would continue to shift between the two parties.

"It has been going back and forth for the last 20 years," he said.

news.title: Gavin Newsom reveals his timeline for deciding 2028 presidential run
news.text:
California Gov. Gavin Newsom said he will decide by early January whether to run for president in 2028, revealing his political timetable during a trip to the COP31 international climate conference in Turkey where he delivered criticism of President Trump.

“I’ll make the determination at the beginning of the year, so we’ll spend the next few weeks with the family and make a decision early January,” Newsom told Turkey’s Anadolu news agency, calling the midterm elections a “rebuke” of Trump. 

Newsom’s remarks elevate yet another international trip in which he praised California’s environmental policies and attacked Trump’s retreat from global climate pacts.

The outgoing governor met with Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva to discuss expanding California’s climate partnership with Brazil, and he finalized a new climate agreement with Portugal, according to the governor’s office.

The governor and his wife Jennifer Siebel Newsom also visited a forestry training center to exchange wildfire lessons, and he joined governors and mayors — including Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz and London Mayor Sadiq Khan — at a gathering convened by U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres.

Newsom’s international globetrotting this year has generally been paid for by wealthy benefactors who fund the California State Protocol Foundation, a nonprofit that has paid for Newsom’s travel expenses instead of taxpayer money.

Newsom and his wife are currently the focus of federal investigations, and feds reportedly requested information about the Protocol Foundation’s donors and fundraisers in subpoenas. Investigators were seeking the governor’s international travel and events, and any money used for the governor’s living and personal expenses, according to the San Francisco Standard.

But new polling suggests the recent election outcomes may not bode well for Newsom, as his chances of winning the Democratic presidential nomination plunged to just 7% in prediction markets. 

Newsom said this month’s election results have placed an obligation on his party to deliver.

“I’m particularly pleased with the outcome of the election, and I think the vast majority of people around the globe are very pleased with the outcome of the election as well,” he said.

For the second consecutive year, the Trump administration did not send a delegation to the annual summit, according to Newsom’s office.

Newsom’s travels also drew a jab from Democratic political strategist Steve Maviglio, who contrasted Gov.-elect Xavier Becerra’s efforts to ingratiate himself with Democratic lawmakers in Sacramento to the outgoing governor’s focus.

“This will be a refreshing change. A Governor who spends time working with the legislature instead of junkets to Turkey,” Maviglio wrote on X.

Newsom has played coy about his presidential ambitions, openly discussing the possibility while leaving himself room to walk away.

In September, Newsom told CNN’s Jake Tapper that he would sit out the 2028 race if former Vice President Kamala Harris entered.

“I don’t know if she runs, but we’ll see,” Newsom said during a fly-fishing interview in Montana. “I wouldn’t run if she ran.”

The claim elicited more than a few eyerolls among those in both Democratic and Republican political circles. But Newsom described a showdown between him and Harris as “mutual assured destruction,” pointing to their overlapping networks of friends and supporters.

“If they’re not on board,” he said, “that’s a non-starter.”

news.title: Democrat Cindy Holscher Wins Kansas Governor’s Race
news.text:
Democratic state Sen. Cindy Holscher has won the Kansas governor’s race, beating Kansas state Senate President Ty Masterson, a Republican.

Holscher, who ran on a campaign of increasing public school funding, lowering property taxes, and expanding Medicaid, won 50.3 percent of the vote compared to Masterson’s 49.7 percent. The Associated Press called the race on Nov. 12.

Up until the final days of the election, Masterson and Holscher were within 2 percentage points of one another in polling. Masterson held a slight lead, with some predictions showing him with around a 65 percent chance of winning.

Current Kansas Gov. Laura Kelly, a Democrat, was unable to seek another term because of term limits. However, in federal elections, Kansas has been largely Republican for decades.

Despite party differences, both candidates proposed deductions in homeowners’ property taxes and highlighted affordability concerns for Kansas voters.

Both focused on improving Kansas education, and both campaigned on attracting businesses and creating more jobs for Kansas.

According to recent polling, disapproval of President Donald Trump has alienated some in Kansas. Top among their concerns are higher prices and the war in Iran.

Trump carried the state in all three of his presidential campaigns, and took it with 57 percent of the vote in 2024.

Some Kansas Republicans seem to have rejected Trump’s sway over the party, and several told The Epoch Times that they switched their votes to Democrats in this election to avoid supporting the president.

Dennis, a voter from Overland Park who declined to share his last name, told The Epoch Times that he is a Republican, but voted for Democrats in both the Senate and governor’s races.

“I’ve been voting Democratic ever since Trump was elected,” Dennis said. “I’m a Bob Dole, Dwight Eisenhower Republican, not a Trumper.”

When asked if he was aware of the shift by his state to the left, Dennis said he believes it’s attributable to dislike of Trump’s policies.

Kelly’s wins in 2018 and 2024 seem to show a path for Democrats to take the state in a Democratic direction. However, in 2020 and 2024, former President Joe Biden and Kamala Harris each only carried the same five counties, among them, the largest in the state: Johnson and Shawnee.

Johnson County voter Deborah Brand is a registered Republican and former Republican committee chairperson, but she has voted largely for Democrats since Trump’s election.

She said she voted for Democrats in the gubernatorial and Senate elections this year because she felt the state “needs checks and balances” that it doesn’t currently have.

However, she said she doesn’t believe that the state’s swing to the left is necessarily permanent.

“Kansas has always been very Republican. I think if there were a decent candidate, they would remain Republican,” she said.
